Qatar Becomes Largest Buyer of U.S. LNG Amid Hormuz Crisis
Qatar is set to become the largest buyer of U.S. LNG, signing long-term deals for 7 million tonnes annually with Cheniere and Woodside.
The Iran war has crippled Qatar's LNG industry, destroying 17% of export capacity, causing $20 billion in annual revenue losses and severely restricting shipments through Hormuz.
QatarEnergy is diversifying away from its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, turning to U.S. LNG supplies to protect its global market position and improve supply reliability.
In an extraordinary turn of events, Qatar, the world’s second-largest LNG exporter before the Iran war, will become the biggest buyer of liquefied natural gas from the United States, the producer that overtook the Gulf nation as top LNG exporter earlier this decade.
This extraordinary turn of events is, of course, the result of the extraordinary disruption that the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz inflicted on Qatar, the LNG producer whose expansion plans for the rest of this decade were rivaled only by the U.S.
The war and the Strait of Hormuz crisis, which is still blocking much of Qatar’s LNG exports, have upended these plans. State-energy firm QatarEnergy is now scrambling to repair the damage at its LNG facilities caused by Iranian missile attacks in March. These attacks took out 17% of Qatar’s export capacity and caused an estimated loss of $20 billion in annual revenue, QatarEnergy said in March.
Seven months later, Qatar is barely moving “very few” cargoes through the Strait of Hormuz as the protracted crisis chokes supply to markets of the LNG volumes that Qatar would have produced, even at reduced capacity.
QatarEnergy has been forced to declare force majeure for up to five years on some long-term LNG contracts. Suddenly, Qatar faces tens of billions of dollars in losses from missed sales. More importantly, the perception that Qatar is a reliable supplier of regular term deliveries has been undermined. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027
The Qatari state-owned energy giant last week extended the force majeure on LNG deliveries to Asia and Europe by another month through the end of December 2026, as LNG cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains largely blocked.
Unlike oil, LNG exporters cannot transport volumes via pipelines, Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, President and CEO of QatarEnergy and Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs, said in September.
“The problem is that LNG, our main export commodity, cannot be transported by pipelines. We will have to transport it by pipelines as gas and then liquify it at receiving terminals wherever that may be,” Al-Kaabi said at the Qatar Economic Forum Special Edition in New York in September.
“This means we are building redundant facilities to the ones we are already building in Qatar as part of the North Field expansion project. This makes no economic sense,” the minister explained, and added, “We have decided not to use pipelines as an alternative based on commercial and technical criteria.”
Referring to resuming LNG production and exports, “Qatar is ready to resume normal operations within a few weeks of the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” the official noted.
As we enter the ninth month of the Hormuz crisis, Qatar is hedging against what could be a forever-changed access through the chokepoint.
“Some shipments are going through the Iranian road to Pakistan, and some are going through the U.S. road to other destinations, but it’s just a few ships that are passing, that were able to pass through the Strait, but it’s not much,” Al-Kaabi said at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York.
With its only route to market blocked, Qatar last month hedged its bets against future disruptions by signing two separate agreements to buy LNG from U.S. producers to diversify its portfolio.
QatarEnergy signed two long-term deals with Cheniere to buy up to 4 million tons per annum of LNG from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi export facilities, with deliveries expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054.
The Qatari firm also signed a long-term agreement to buy 3 million tons per annum of LNG from Woodside Energy’s Louisiana LNG project, which is currently under construction. Deliveries on a free-on-board (FOB) basis are set to begin in 2030 for 20 years.
“These additional volumes make QatarEnergy the largest buyer of LNG from the U.S., and place us in a stronger position to meet the global growing needs for LNG,” QatarEnergy’s Al-Kaabi said .
“Our Golden Pass LNG project and our expanding portfolio of U.S. LNG purchases reinforce QatarEnergy’s leadership in the LNG industry and support our long-term growth and diversification strategy.”
With Hormuz out of the picture in the near term and uncertainty about disruptions in the longer term, Qatar is expanding its LNG supply options with deliveries from its biggest rival, the United States.
The deal with Woodside “reflects QatarEnergy’s continued confidence in the long-term role of LNG in the global energy mix and its strategy to further develop a flexible, diversified and globally competitive LNG portfolio,” the Qatari firm said, as the Iran war fundamentally changed the global LNG supply market in both availability and reliability.

Iran War and AI Boom Drive Global Gas Supply Crunch
Asian LNG prices have more than tripled to over $31/MMBtu, as Europe and Asia compete for scarce supplies following the disruption of Qatari exports.
The Iran war has wiped out an estimated 60 billion cubic meters of LNG supply, with the IEA forecasting a record 3% decline in global production this year.
The LNG crunch could persist well into 2027, as growing AI-driven power demand, limited supply growth and Qatar's prolonged export disruptions keep markets tight.
LNG spot market prices in Asia have tripled since the start of the year. Asia and Europe are locked in a race for a limited number of cargoes. The U.S. is exporting record volumes of the fuel. And QatarEnergy just extended a force majeure on its own LNG exports. The world is short on gas—and will remain so for a while.
The Japan-Korea Marker, the Asian LNG benchmark, topped $31 per million British thermal units this month. In fact, the benchmark briefly rose above $33 per mmBtu, compared with a little over $9 per mmBtu in January this year. The price change speaks volumes about the impact of the war in the Persian Gulf on global gas supply security, as it took one of the top three liquefied gas exporters off the market.
Replacing Qatar has proven difficult, even for the United States, which has boosted its LNG exports substantially, thanks mostly to strong demand from Europe, which has few alternatives to Qatari LNG, unlike Asia, which has the alternative of coal and is taking advantage of it. Still, gas supply is tight and will remain tight next year as well, the International Energy Agency warned this week.
The war between the United States and Israel, and Iran, cost the world some 60 billion cu m in LNG supply losses in the eight months to October, the IEA has estimated. Higher production in the United States and Africa helped fill much of that gap—as much as two-thirds. Alas, two-thirds is not 100%, so a gap remains, and the IEA expects global LNG production to decline by 3% this year, with the March-October period seeing a 6% drop. A 3% supply decline might not seem like much, but it would be the steepest annual drop since records began—and it comes as demand expectations rise amid the AI race. Related: IEA Warns Global Gas Crunch Could Last Well into 2027
Until the war in the Middle East began, the outlook for natural gas generally and LNG specifically was exceptionally bullish thanks to the boom in data center construction as Big Tech prioritizes artificial intelligence as its number-one growth engine for the future. Data centers, it was quickly discovered, cannot be powered reliably by alternative energy sources such as wind and solar, even with batteries. The most viable—and quickest—option was natural gas.
Based on these demand trends, Shell said in its LNG Outlook 2026 that it expected demand for liquefied gas to surge by 65% between this year and 2050—despite the disruption in Qatari exports caused by the war. “The conflict created a system-wide shock with disruption cascading across all segments of the economy, but the LNG industry has proved resilient and able to adapt to changing market conditions,” Shell’s head of natural gas operations said at the time.
The LNG industry has indeed adapted, mostly through production ramp-ups at existing facilities or plans for additional capacity that just a year ago was flagged as potentially surplus and leading to a major LNG supply glut. But with the war still quite hot and Qatari gas still unavailable, nobody is talking about a glut anymore. Qatar has taken an interesting approach to securing long-term supply.
In recent weeks, the country's state energy company closed two long-term LNG supply deals with U.S. companies. One deal is for 4 million tons of LNG annually from Cheniere Energy. The other is for 3 million tons annually from Woodside Energy. This, according to Reuters, will make QatarEnergy the biggest foreign buyer of U.S. liquefied gas. QatarEnergy has expansion plans, and a force majeure on domestic production is not going to get in the way. This signals confidence in the resilience of LNG demand—even as some question it.
Energy Intelligence recently voiced the suggestion that the war-related price surge could dampen demand for liquefied natural gas, in line with historical patterns in oil and other commodities, energy and otherwise. However, it could be counter-argued that any demand dampening in LNG would be, first, limited, and, second, temporary because demand for energy commodities tends to be rather inelastic.
Indeed, demand is already down. The IEA reported that over the first nine months of the year, total gas consumption globally went down—but it went down by just 1% or 35 billion cu m. This is not a proportional decline to the squeeze in supply, in evidence of that inelasticity above. It is also evidence that the long-term outlook for LNG and gas in general is rightly optimistic. Unfortunately for those concerned about the relative emission output of gas and coal, so is the outlook for coal, because coal is cheaper than gas.

If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett's 7-Word Investing Advice Has Never Been Wrong
Stocks have been shaky in recent weeks, with the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES: ^DJI), and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) slipping by around 3%, 4%, and 8%, respectively, from their recent all-time highs.
Investors are also feeling pessimistic about the future. The Fear and Greed Index measures investor sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, with lower numbers indicating fear and higher values suggesting greed. As of this writing, the index sits at just 23 -- in the "extreme fear" category.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
If a stock market crash is coming, it's not all bad news for investors. Warren Buffett has a simple seven-word strategy for times like these, and it could help you generate life-changing wealth amid market volatility.
Image source: Getty Images. Bad news is an investor's best friend
In 2008, Buffett penned an opinion piece for The New York Times . The U.S. was deep into the Great Recession at that point, with the S&P 500 having plunged nearly 40% over the previous year, and many investors were losing hope that the market would ever recover.
In the essay, Buffett encouraged investors to not only stay in the market, but to buy more. He noted that the market had endured severe hardship over the previous century and still managed to deliver record-shattering returns. Those who reaped the biggest rewards were the investors who continued buying.
"[B]ad news is an investor's best friend," he emphasized. "It lets you buy a slice of America's future at a marked-down price."
Since that piece was published, the S&P 500 has earned total returns of more than 1,000%. In other words, if you'd invested $10,000 in an S&P 500 ETF the day Buffett offered this advice, you'd have more than $112,000 by today.
"You might think it would have been impossible for an investor to lose money during a century marked by such an extraordinary gain," Buffett continued, discussing the Dow's meteoric rise from 66 to 11,497. "But some investors did. The hapless ones bought stocks only when they felt comfort in doing so and then proceeded to sell when the headlines made them queasy."
History says this is the best move investors can make
If the headlines are making you queasy right now, that's understandable. But the right investments can set you up for lucrative long-term returns, even if a crash or recession is coming.
Not all stocks are strong enough to weather a significant downturn. During the dot-com bubble burst, for example, countless tech companies crashed and never recovered. Many powerful companies collapsed during the Great Recession, too. Whenever the next bear market begins, there will inevitably be some companies that don't pull through.
Organizations with strong foundations are the most likely to succeed. These companies will have sustainable competitive advantages, sound finances, competent leadership teams, and other factors that set them apart from their peers.
"To be sure, investors are right to be wary of highly leveraged entities or businesses in weak competitive positions. But fears regarding the long-term prosperity of the nation's many sound companies make no sense. These businesses will indeed suffer earnings hiccups, as they always have. But most major companies will be setting new profit records 5, 10 and 20 years from now."-Warren Buffett, The New York Times (2008)
Over time, the market is all but guaranteed to thrive. Since 1919, the S&P 500 has ended every one of its rolling 20-year periods with positive total returns. This means that if you'd invested in the S&P 500 at any point in the last century and held your investment for 20 years, you'd have made money.
Nobody can say when the next market crash or recession is coming, but strong companies are the most likely to thrive over time. With a healthy portfolio and a long-term outlook, you can set yourself up for lucrative gains.

items.title: US midterm results a 'victory' for Canadians hopeful of tariff relief
items.summary: With Canada-US trade talks back on, Tuesday’s midterm Democratic wave puts pressure on the White House to come to a deal.
items.content:
Image caption, US tariffs on Canada featured heavily in Michigan and Maine, where Democratic candidates won big on Tuesday
It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies.
"I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".
Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.
US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and a survey by the Cato Institute in September , external suggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.
In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.
In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.
She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.

In Ohio, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Jon Husted, called the levies a "disaster" and vowed to slash costs for voters by getting rid of them , external .
Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.
Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.
And speaking to Fox News on Tuesday night, Trump touted his "ultimate power" of veto to shut down bills passed by Congress that he does not like.
Some Democratic lawmakers have also supported certain tariffs in the past as a way to protect American manufacturing jobs, and could back keeping some in place.
Figure caption, How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.
After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (Â£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.
The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.
Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.
Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by â raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.
There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.
Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.
On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon".
"Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.
Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservatives, said on Wednesday that "nobody controls Donald Trump".
But he said that midterms results show Canada has "massive leverage" given that the tariffs are broadly unpopular.
"We've got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade," he said.
Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Trump may indeed feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."
But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.
Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.
After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.
And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

items.title: Sharp objects found in Halloween sweets in three European nations
items.summary: Dozens of cases are reported in Austria, Germany and Hungary, including a nine-year-old girl hurting her tongue while eating chocolate containing a pin.
items.content:
Needles and other sharp metal objects have been found in sweets handed out over Halloween in Germany, Austria and Hungary, prompting police to issue warnings to parents to check what their children have been given.
Police in a number of German states have reported cases, from Bavaria in the south-east to Lower Saxony in the north.
A girl aged nine hurt her tongue while eating a chocolate bar in BremervÃ¶rde, west of Hamburg. A 5cm-long (2in) pin was then found inside it.
Meanwhile, police in Hungary have launched a criminal investigation after nails, screws and pieces of wire were found in sweets handed out to children who had been trick-or-treating in and around the town of GyÃ¶mrÅ, to the east of Budapest.
The local authority said one young girl had been handed a toffee with a nail inside a chocolate wrapper and that she had fortunately noticed in time and had not swallowed the sweet.
Several cases have also been reported across Austria, where Interior Minister Gerhard Karner condemned the incidents as "cowardly, malicious and in some cases life-threatening".
Image caption, A chocolate wrapper was used to hand a girl a toffee with a sharp tack inside it in Hungary
Police there said investigations were under way in four states, and that a 10-year-old girl had suffered a minor injury to her mouth when she bit into a small chocolate bar in the Amstetten area to the east of Linz.
Lower Austria Governor Johanna Mikl-Leitner said the perpetrators had to feel the full force of the law, adding: "Our children deserve a carefree childhood and we'll continue to ensure that."
Warning after 'metal pins' found in Halloween sweets
German police in the south-eastern state of Bavaria said that, while there had been similar cases reported in the past two years, initial figures this year suggested a significant increase in incidents.
As many as 25 cases involving sweets containing needles, screws or nails have been reported by police in Bavaria.
Police in the Middle Franconia region of western Bavaria have also warned of the risk of copycat actions, after a mother found a needle in her child's chocolate bar and reported it to police.
She later returned to the police to say her child had admitted to inserting the needle.

items.title: What Republicans' huge loss means for Trump
items.summary: Trump's handling of tariffs, the Iran war and an array of Washington-area construction projects are sure to face sudden pushback from newly empowered Democrats.
items.content:
What Republicans' huge loss means for Donald Trump
Democrats won sweeping midterm election victories in the House and Senate, shaking up Washington and putting President Donald Trump in a bind.
Trump still wields significant presidential powers and has strongly signaled that he plans to veto Democratic bills.
Democrats plan to launch a slew of investigations that are widely expected to consume much of the rest of Trump's term.
Democrats just put President Donald Trump in a bind.
The party is projected to win commanding majorities in the House and Senate after thrashing Republicans in key races up and down the ballot across the country. The blue tsunami will knock Washington on its head and crush the Republican congressional bulwark that both supported and shielded Trump through the first two years of his term.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
The midterm result snuffs out any chance Trump had of passing partisan legislation in the second half of his presidency. And many of the interests he has been able to pursue without Congress' input — including tariffs , the Iran war and an array of Washington-area construction projects — are sure to face sudden pushback from newly empowered Democratic majorities.
The paradigm shift hardly leaves Trump helpless, however. As president at a time of executive power expansion , Trump wields singular authorities that could stymie Democrats' efforts to pursue their own agendas.
Live updates: Day 2 of 2026 midterm election results
The economy brought Trump back to power. Now it's his downfall
Democrats take Congress in a blue wave. Here's what it means for your money
A blow to billionaire donors and a reckoning for tech companies — 5 takeaways
Analysis: The Democrats have one chance to extract concessions from Trump. Markets will hate it
What Trump losing power over Congress means for Iran, Ukraine and foreign policy
Elon Musk's record election bet backfired. The backlash may reach beyond one billionaire
But with his grip on the Capitol shriveling and his approval ratings scraping record lows in numerous polls, it's unclear how much support he'll be able to muster to fight the coming political battles.
Even before Election Day, analysts and pundits had contemplated a Democratic rout so decisive that it would force a reckoning for the GOP, and potentially even pose an existential threat to Trump's "Make America Great Again" movement.
Marc Short, chairman of Advancing American Freedom and onetime chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence , told CNBC on Tuesday afternoon that the GOP has moved away from its conservative foundations.
"We need a refresh right now," Short said in an interview. "We've lost our way."
Trump has been vague about what he hopes to achieve with the rest of his term. But he has shared a vision of how he might coexist with a Democratic majority, and it involves heavy use of the veto pen.
"It's one of the stronger powers that a president has," Trump said in a Fox News interview overnight. "They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them."
"And after a couple of months of vetoes, they'll call and they'll say, 'How do we get this stuff done?' And we'll work together," he said, adding, "I have a lot of friends that are Democrats."
Trump has previously stated his willingness to veto reams of legislation that Democrats send across his desk. In a New York Post podcast interview released Monday, Trump said that if Republicans don't win, "I veto everything."
Pressed to detail his plans for the next two years, Trump touted his record and said, "The most important thing is to keep it going. It's going to get better and better and better, unless people come in that hate our country."
If that happens, "I guess I'll become Mr. Veto," Trump said.
He may soon get his chance: House Democrats, poised to be led by current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, are planning to pass a flurry of bills as soon as they take the reins next January, CNBC has learned.
The legislative push, first reported by The New York Times, aims to show a united Democratic caucus taking quick action on the issues they were elected to solve, especially oppressively high costs on everything from gas to groceries.
In their first 100 hours after being sworn in, House Democrats plan to introduce bills reinstating the enhanced health insurance subsidies that expired under the GOP-held Congress, and reversing the Medicaid cuts Trump signed into law earlier this year.
Democrats also plan to push forward a bill that would undo Trump's sweeping tariffs and reassert Congress' role in setting import taxes. And they will again vote on legislation to end the war with Iran, or seek congressional authorization to keep it going.
But without Trump's approval, those bills may end up as little more than symbolic gestures, as Democrats will lack the two-thirds majorities in both chambers that are required to override a presidential veto without GOP help.
And there's no guarantee the bills will even make it out of Congress: Despite their landslide victories, Senate Democrats will still end up shy of the 60 votes required to bypass the chamber's filibuster rules for most legislation, giving Republicans key leverage in the minority.
Democrats also could feasibly benefit from Trump's vetoes in the long term. Forcing the president to shoot down numerous popular bills could give them fodder in the 2028 election.
It's far from clear whether Trump believes he can find compromise with Democrats on any of their initial legislative priorities.
But any potential for a working relationship with the opposition could be poisoned early on, as Democrats in both chambers are aggressively signaling their plans to launch politically charged investigations against Trump, his political and corporate allies and even his family members.
Winning control of House committees gives Democrats the ability to issue subpoenas under the current rules .
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is likely to chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, said his panel will target the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption and alleged abuses by federal immigration agencies. He also plans to return focus to the Trump administration's handling of files related to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, Garcia summed up his plans in a two-word statement : "Lawyer up."
It's not just Garcia. Other Democrats have already demanded records from the Trump administration on a range of issues. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., for instance, last week accused Trump of using tariff exemptions to cut " sweetheart deals " for industries whose leaders have plied the president with gifts .
"They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we'll be printing," Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said in an X post late Tuesday in response to a post, appearing to refer to tech executives.
The investigations are widely expected to consume much of the rest of Trump's term.
Trump has ample experience being targeted by Democrats, who impeached him twice in the House during his first presidential term.
But with his base of support appearing to erode inside and outside of Washington, Trump may have to face his political foes with a smaller arsenal than he's used to.
"I'm not expecting Republicans to revolt" against Trump following the midterm losses, AAF's Short told CNBC. "But I'm expecting some of them to quietly distance themselves."

items.title: Stock market today: Dow rallies 1,500 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gain after Democrats win control of Congress - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Stock market today: Dow rallies 1,500 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gain after Democrats win control of Congress
items.content:
Stock market today: Dow surges 1,500 points in best day of 2026, S&P 500 and Nasdaq rally after historic midterm election
Updated Wed, November 4, 2026 at 2:07 PM MST 2 min read
US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 3%, or over 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed 1.6%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) traded up by 1.4% amid a post-election relief rally.
Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction . Chip stocks, including Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Micron ( MU ), fell. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses, with Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) each hitting all-time highs.
Oil prices plunged as the midterm election outcome also raised hopes for an end to the war in the Middle East. Brent crude oil futures ( BZ=F ) dropped 8% to around $95 per barrel.
Investors will also be watching in the coming weeks for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election. As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday , midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term.
On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring , meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated "pretty solid job growth."
Earnings continue to roll in. AMD ( AMD ) posted a Q3 earnings beat , while McDonald's ( MCD ) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth . Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth.
Dow surges 3% as stocks rally after midterm elections
US stocks rallied Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, as investors embraced the prospect of divided government and rotated into several of the market's biggest technology names.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 3%, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025.
Meanwhile, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 1.5%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) climbed 1.4%.
Oil prices plunged amid the rally in stocks, with West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) falling more than 7.7% below $90 a barrel.
Duolingo stock soars 30% after Q3 earnings give shares a much-needed jolt
Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock has recovered nearly all of its year-to-date losses after a strong earnings report eased concerns about the company's growth. Shares of the language learning app are up nearly 30% on the day.
In the third quarter, Duolingo reported that its daily active users (DAUs) rose 29% year over year to 64.9 million. Paid subscribers for the language learning platform grew 14% annually to 13.1 million.
Investors also cheered management's note that the company will be "gradually leaning more into monetization in ways that preserve the quality of our free experience."
"In our view, the quarter begins to address the primary investor concern following second-quarter results: whether accelerating engagement can translate into stronger monetization," William Blair analysts led by Ralph Schackart wrote in a note. "DAU growth accelerated for a second consecutive quarter, subscription bookings reaccelerated meaningfully, and management expects paid-subscriber growth to bottom in a couple of quarters as the stronger bookings trajectory flows through revenue."
Stocks rise but fueled by cyclical and defensive sectors
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed on Wednesday, powered by cyclical and defensive stocks.
Consumer Discretionary, which houses e-commerce giant Amazon ( AMZN ), led the gains, followed closely by Communications Services, which includes tech giant Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ). Shares of Amazon rallied 7% while Alphabet rose more than 4%.
Financials ( XLF ) also rallied, along with defensive sectors like Consumer Staples( XLP ), Real Estate ( XLRE ), and Health Care ( XLV ).
Investors continued to rotate out of tech, even as it was up modestly on Wednesday. Political headwinds for the AI buildout and tumbling oil prices gave way to breadth outside semiconductor stocks, which have been the high fliers this year.
Wall Street's post-midterm party has two no-shows: the AI/chip trade and oil, which is having a far worse time.
West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) is back under $90 a barrel. It has given up about $15 since Friday's $104 close and is on pace for its worst week since April 2020. The slide came as traders bet on an end to the Iran war after Tuesday's elections.
Brent ( BZ=F ) is near a two-month low. Gasoline futures ( RB=F ) are on track for their lowest close since March 10, which is welcome news for anyone driving to Thanksgiving dinner. Energy stocks ( XLE ) are down more than 5%, with refiners taking the biggest hit.
Still, crude remains about 50% above where it started the year. US diesel stockpiles are at their lowest since 2003, and the Wells Fargo Investment Institute says gasoline and diesel supplies "remain constrained by the war."
Nationwide's Mark Hackett says oil is retreating "on hopes for a deescalation in the Iran conflict, even as the diplomatic signals remain ambiguous."
Watch whether WTI settles under $90 at 2:30 p.m. ET.
Trump Media stock plunges after Democrats sweep Congress
Voters on Tuesday delivered a stunning rebuke to the Trump agenda, but markets produced a referendum of their own — on the president's eponymous stock, Hamza Shaban reports:
Trump Media & Technology Group ( DJT ) stock, the home of the president's Truth Social platform, plunged over 12% during morning trading Wednesday. The ticker has served as a bellwether of the president's power, reflecting his outsized influence over all things politics, and his ability to attract capital and attention.
But the election results have shifted the balance of power. Democratic victories in battleground states and formerly Trump-voting districts have shattered the GOP's trifecta hold on Washington. And they have called into question Trump's own standing and effectiveness as party leader, chief executive, and business mogul.
Bitcoin rises above $80,000 as investors go risk-on
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) jumped 3%, and ethereum ( ETH-USD ) also rallied on Wednesday after Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, even as the midterm outcome could complicate the crypto industry's efforts to pass favorable legislation.
Bitcoin touched a six-week low before recovering to just above $80,000, moving back above its 50-day moving average. Ethereum also rallied, gaining 7% to trade above $2,400 as US equities broadly rallied and investors went risk-on.
Uber ( UBER ) reported third quarter results on Wednesday that topped estimates, but rising costs and weakness in the Middle East are expected to hit Q4 profit performance, Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Uber forecast fourth quarter adjusted ​EPS of $0.95 to $0.99, below estimates of $1.06. The company said the Middle East conflict was a 75-basis-point drag on mobility bookings and could be 100 basis points in Q4.
"Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a statement.
AI's circular financing is a 'feature,' not a bug, Wall Street bond committee tells Treasury
The cost of insuring AI borrowers' debt has jumped as much as 80% since August.
The government's top bond advisers say the money sloshing around the AI boom is built that way on purpose, and that it's mostly fine — at least for now, Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre reports:
The Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee , a panel of big-bank and investor executives that advises Treasury on how the US borrows, made AI debt one of its two research topics this quarter. Its presentation , out Wednesday, sums up the view in one slide title: "Circular Financing is a feature."
That's the loop of chipmakers, cloud companies and their biggest customers funding one another. The committee's bet is that the hardware outlasts some of its buyers. "While some individual compute operators might not remain viable, the physical infrastructure will continue to find demand," the presentation said.
Apple, Microsoft hit all-time highs as Nasdaq surges 2% in post-election rally
Stocks surged on Wednesday, with most sectors green across the board after a Democratic mid-term election sweep.
Tech ( XLK ) bounced as Apple ( AAPL ) shares hit all-time highs, sending the iPhone maker's market cap above $5 trillion. Microsoft ( MSFT ) also surged 6% to hit a new record. The Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) composite rallied more than 2%, while the Dow ( ^DJI ) surged more than 1,100 points, or about 2%.
Why the stock market is unexpectedly rallying in the wake of the Democratic blue wave
Call it a contrarian move, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
It has been a riveting 12 hours or so in the markets as investors slice and dice the midterm election outcomes.
Initially, stocks got hammered as the results trickled in. The thinking was that Democrats are less pro-business than Republicans, and since they will control the House and the Senate, there goes the corporate profit miracle that has driven the markets over the past two years.
But something very interesting has emerged after that initial knee-jerk reaction. Stocks are rallying on Wednesday — big-time!
US services growth slows in October as inflation pressures persist
US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as growth moderated and businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs and supply chain disruptions.
The Institute for Supply Management's services index fell to 54.5 from 54.9 in September, missing economists' expectations of 54.8, though still marking its 28th consecutive month in expansion territory.
New orders dropped 3.9 points to 55.9 as business activity ebbed. Employment picked up for a second consecutive month, with its index rising to 51.4 from 50.1.
Meanwhile, a measure of prices paid eased to 73.0 from 74.0 but remained elevated as businesses faced higher fuel costs, tariffs and shipping delays.
A separate survey from S&P Global also showed slower growth, with its services index falling to 56.1 from 58.8 in September. Businesses reported strong demand but raised selling prices more quickly as they passed on higher operating costs.
Apple hits new high. Why the Democratic blue wave may be good for the stock.
Apple ( AAPL ) stock jumped 6% to a new all-time high on Wednesday as investors perceived the stock as a winner from the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi breaks down what analysts are saying is behind the move higher:
One winner could be Apple ( AAPL ) for two reasons, opined Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani.
The first is more of a defensive play amid the unknown that is fresh D.C. gridlock.
"Apple offers a different earnings driver through iPhone mix/pricing and services rather than data-center construction; our work points to resilient demand, with gross-margin recovery and price elasticity the key tests. This is THE name to keep working when investors want to get defensive," Daryanani said.
The other aspect is cooling memory chip prices, a major headwind for Apple, as data center projects get delayed or outright blocked by the Dems.
Daryanani added, "Memory input inflation (DRAM & NAND) has been a sizable headwind for a host of names in our coverage (AAPL for example, talked about 140bps GM headwind in Dec-qtr due to memory, but also PC names). Could a slowdown in DC buildouts actually temper memory demand and, in a way, help companies that have been impacted by the sizable memory inflation (AAPL is the key one but there are many others)?"
US stocks opened higher Wednesday as investors digested Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress along with fresh earnings and economic data.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 2%, while those on the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) climbed 1.1% each.
Investors are also weighing what business policy shifts election results could bring to specific sectors, including possible moves on housing, pharmaceuticals, and data center construction. Chip stocks also came under pressure, with Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Micron ( MU ) lower, while AMD ( AMD ) slipped after its quarterly results.
'Pretty solid job growth:' Private US employers added 86,000 jobs in October
Hiring in the private sector showed continued strength in October, according to payroll processor ADP, as employers across a variety of industries added roles , Yahoo Finance's Claire Boston reports:
Private companies added 86,000 jobs this month, matching a revised 86,000 in September, data released Wednesday showed. Economists had been expecting a gain of 67,000 jobs.
Base wages for private-sector workers rose 3.2%, a figure that still trails inflation , while gross pay, which includes additional compensation such as overtime and bonuses, was up 4.7%.
"You have back-to-back, two consecutive straight months of pretty solid job growth," ADP chief economist Nela Richardson said.
Block stock jumps as Jack Dorsey's AI bet shows signs of paying off
Eight months after Jack Dorsey made one of corporate America's boldest bets on shrinking its workforce to prepare for the age of artificial intelligence, investors are finding more reasons to buy into the Silicon Valley billionaire's pivot.
Shares of Dorsey's Block ( XYZ ), the payments company behind Cash App and merchant processor Square, jumped 9% in premarket trading Wednesday after it reported better-than-expected third quarter earnings and raised its gross profit outlook for next year.
McDonald's Q3 sales growth slows amid tough consumer backdrop, new drinks push
McDonald's ( MCD ) sales growth slowed in the third quarter as consumers faced a challenging economic backdrop and the fast food chain unveiled its growth strategy.
The results showed that same-store sales grew by 1.5% year over year, a tick above the 1.4% growth Wall Street expected, according to Bloomberg estimates. In Q3 last year, McDonald's posted same-store sales growth of 3.6%.
In the US, the company posted a 0.2% decline in comparable sales, slightly narrower than the expected 0.5% drop. Data from Placer.ai showed visits to the Golden Arches declined from a year ago, but the company said customers spent more when they did go.
Promotions in October led to some strength ahead of the holiday season. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company is "encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value."
CVS announces plan to split into 2 companies, separating pharmacy from insurance
CVS ( CVS ) announced plans to separate into two independent, publicly traded companies on Wednesday, reshaping one of the largest healthcare companies in the US.
The company intends to separate CVS Health's insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and healthcare services operations from its retail pharmacy and community healthcare segments.
The planned separation represents a significant shift from CVS Health's long-term strategy of bringing together insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and direct healthcare services under a single corporate structure.
Under the proposed structure, one company will retain the CVS Health name and house Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.
The second entity, which will operate under the name CVS Pharmacy, will include approximately 9,000 retail pharmacy locations and MinuteClinic locations, among other services.
Democrats won control of Congress. Their economic agenda is set to target healthcare, tariffs, and Trump's allies.
Democrats retook power in Washington on Tuesday night after flipping key House and Senate seats to command majorities in both houses of Congress.
Democrats secured control of the Senate after winning races in historically red states including Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas.
The party was also "marching toward control of the U.S. House" late Tuesday night, according to the Associated Press, after flipping seats from Florida to New Jersey to Kentucky. All four major networks said Democrats' control of the House was assured.
The power shift creates a new platform for Democrats to launch investigations of President Trump's economic allies — Elon Musk to name one — and pass bills that may be unlikely to become law but will mark a sharp change in the political climate for business leaders and economic issues after two years of unified Republican control.
The change also appears set to elevate figures like Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren and others to prominent positions with oversight over economic policy.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., talks with reporters during a midterm election night phone bank and watch party in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) · Tom Williams via Getty Images
The AI sell-off saved Apple from a sell-off of its own
Despite an earnings beat and strong iPhone sales, investors focused on Apple's ( AAPL ) weaknesses, slowing services growth, and projected lower margins as the stock fell 2% on Tuesday.
But the iPhone maker may have also been cushioned by its unique position among the tech giants — and the massive sell-off they had just a few trading days ago.
While everyone else has been spending lavishly on the AI build-out, Apple has been biding its time , as if content to let its competitors simply do their business on its hardware. To some, this is the "wrong" end of the AI trade.
But in the jittery moments of AI angst, when that lavish spending's meaning shifts from "potential" to "risk," it sends investors running from Google, Amazon, and Microsoft into the arms of Cupertino, safe from the risky AI bets .
A Democrat won the Texas governor's race after promising to halt new data center construction
A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state's first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies.
The state is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers.
Incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott conceded the race late Tuesday, calling Hinojosa and then telling his supporters , "mathematically we are not going to be able to win this election." The Associated Press declared Hinojosa the winner at 11:17 p.m. ET.
Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.
Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa makes a final public appearance with supporters outside the Austin Recreation Center before polls closed on Election Day, Nov. 3, 2026, in Austin, Texas. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images) · Chip Somodevilla via Getty Images

items.title: Spain’s deadly train crashes have damaged public confidence in the system
items.summary: Pedro Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are racing to rebuild trust ahead of a snap election, but the task they face is immense• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereA week ago today, for the second time in nine months, I got in my car and drove south from Madrid to cover a deadly train crash
items.content:
Spain is trying to recover from another train disaster on the brink of an election. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP
Spain is trying to recover from another train disaster on the brink of an election. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP
Spain’s deadly train crashes have damaged public confidence in the system
Pedro Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are racing to rebuild trust ahead of a snap election, but the task they face is immense
Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
A week ago today, for the second time in nine months, I got in my car and drove south from Madrid to cover a deadly train crash.
At 8.53am last Wednesday, a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state-owned rail company, Renfe, smashed into the back of a stationary train run by the private rail company Iryo, on the outskirts of the small town of Urda in Castilla-La Mancha. Sixty-nine people died in the accident , more than 100 were injured, and Spain’s already depleted confidence in its treasured rail network plummeted.
As I drove to Urda, I – along with much of Spain – was feeling a grim sense of deja vu. On 18 January, an Iryo train on the same line from Madrid to Seville had derailed near the Andalucían town of Adamuz before being struck by a Renfe train coming from the opposite direction. Forty-six people died, scores were injured and public trust in Spain’s trains was badly shaken.
The things I saw and heard in Urda mirrored those I’d seen and heard in Adamuz : local people rushing to the train tracks to help the injured; the rapid repurposing of municipal halls into emergency triage centres; and all manner of spontaneous acts of selflessness, bravery, practicality and compassion.
Some of the passengers whose journey south had come to a violent and premature end near Urda stood in line, many still with their wheelie cases and rucksacks, waiting for the coaches that had been chartered to take them onward. The queues looked almost normal until you noticed the odd bandaged head, torn trouser leg, or bloodstained top.
Josimar Medina, a young Peruvian who was travelling with his Brazilian girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, told me the blood on his brown T-shirt belonged to an American called Austin. Medina had helped free Austin from the wreckage and had managed to get him out of the train.
Although the young American was badly hurt, Medina had seen far worse injuries as he clambered off the train. “I saw … people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” he said . “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”
The shock and sorrow has echoed around Spain as the country tries to come to terms with what has happened, and to accept that its extensive and modern speed rail system – long a source of national pride – may not be the safe and reliable network it once seemed.
As the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, put it last week , “public trust in the high-speed system has been broken”.
Sánchez and his socialist-led coalition government are now racing to rebuild that trust, but the task they face is immense – especially given the current circumstances.
Pedro Sánchez is leading a country in mourning. Photograph: GSLV/GTRES/Shutterstock The anger and grief are still raw and, with a snap general election now less than a month away, the political atmosphere is explosive. The prime minister’s critics point out that 115 people died at Adamuz and Urda, and Sánchez and his ministers have had eight years to focus on, and invest in, rail safety. On Tuesday evening, the transport minister, Óscar Puente, accepted the inevitable, announcing his resignation , with the acknowledgment that “neither the country, nor I, can bear 100 deaths in less than a year”.
With the election drawing closer, the language from opposition parties is becoming more strident.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP), which is expected to finish first in next month’s vote, has accused the Sánchez administration of failing to keep Spaniards safe and of trying to use the latest tragedy to political ends.
“It’s not just obvious that they’re not good at being in charge,” Feijóo said on Monday . “It’s that I’m also not sure that they’re good people, either.”
The far-right Vox party, with whom the PP could form a national coalition government, has been even more scathing, accusing the government of “killing” the train crash victims and of “incompetence, corruption, cronyism, and a lack of investment in maintenance and infrastructure improvements”. It is also urging the supreme court to investigate Puente on suspicion of manslaughter and causing bodily harm through gross negligence. Puente has rejected allegations of mismanagement, and has insisted that Spain’s railway system is “safe and reliable”.
Despite signs of a modest resurgence in support just before the latest crash, Sánchez always faced a tough road to re-election. Corruption scandals have bedevilled his inner circle and his government was much criticised for its response to the mass crossing into Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta over the summer. That road now looks even more impassable.
But with disasters, emergencies and deaths so frequently politicised, especially in Spain, the worry now is that solutions to the failings at Adamuz and Urda may be missed amid all the campaigning and point-scoring.
As the politicians bicker and Spain prepares for its fifth general election in 10 years, the long process of recovery is just beginning for some of those who survived last week’s crash.
On Saturday afternoon, I got an email from the family of Austin Hartman, the young American pulled out of the train by Josimar Medina. They told me that Austin, a Cal Poly State University student who had been studying in Madrid, was being treated in a Spanish hospital for multiple fractures to his pelvis, hip, femur, humerus and rib, and was unlikely to be well enough to return home for at least two months. GoFundMe pages have been set up for Austin and his friend Leah Silver-Fajardo , who was also badly hurt in the accident.
His family had seen the photo I took of Josimar and Vitoria in Urda and wanted to know if there was any way of contacting them so that Austin could say thank you. By the following day, Austin and his family had video called the couple.
“It was so helpful for us to … thank Josimar for treating Austin with such loving care when he needed it more than anything,” Austin’s stepmother, Sandi, told me in an email on Tuesday. “Austin credits him with saving his life. As we know, beautiful things are born of tragedy and it’s usually in the relationships that are formed out of it.”

items.title: Rwanda's army team removed from Africa league after US sanctions, NBA says
items.summary: The US imposed sanctions on Rwanda's army over its role in the conflict in DR Congo.
items.content:
Image caption, Rwanda's army team APR came third in the Basketball Africa League last year
The National Basketball Association (NBA) says it removed Rwanda's army team from its African league because of US sanctions imposed on the country in March.
The NBA had previously said the Rwandan army-funded ArmÃ©e Patriotique Rwandaise (APR) club would not participate in the 2026 Basketball Africa League (BAL).
However this is the first time the NBA has revealed the reasons behind the APR's removal.
The association was responding to complaints by two US senators, who sent a letter asking them to reconsider their partnership with the Rwandan team. The US placed sanctions on the Rwandan army, accusing it of fuelling the conflict in the Democratic Republic of Congo in March.
The senators said the NBA risked "becoming complicit in sportswashing by accepting money from a Rwandan government that systematically abuses human rights".
Last week, the US also imposed sanctions on Rwanda's defence ministry over its support for the M23 rebel group which has seized control of large parts of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies backing the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
Rwanda is an official BAL partner and pays the league to host its finals at the 10,000-seat BK Arena in the capital, Kigali.
The evidence that shows Rwanda is backing rebels in DR Congo
In the letter to the NBA dated 23 October, Democratic Senator Jeffrey Merkley and Republican counterpart Marsha Blackburn gave the association until 2 November to give a written response regarding its continued partnership with Rwanda.
"What is the NBA red line for accepting money from foreign governments that commit human rights abuses?" the senators asked.
Among other queries, they also questioned how the association could "reconcile its continued partnership with Rwanda with its purported commitment to justice".
In its response, NBA deputy commissioner Mark Tatum said the Rwandan team "had been withdrawn" from the BAL following the sanctions imposed earlier in the year, American sports website ESPN reports.
The NBA said the APR basketball club would remain barred while the US sanctions are in place.
The APR is one of Rwanda's top basketball teams and represented the country in the BAL in 2024 and 2025, when it came third. It was replaced by the RSSB Tigers this year.
The BAL is a pan-African basketball league established and co-organised by the NBA and the basketball's world governing body Fiba.
It is a professional league featuring 12 club teams from across the continent.
Rwanda has hosted all but one of the league's final and playoff matches since the inaugural match in 2021.
The NBA reportedly receives millions of dollars annually from the country for the marketing and partnership rights.
DR Congo has repeatedly condemned Rwanda's high-profile international sports deals, including with the NBA, European football clubs and Formula 1, asking them to end their campaigns.
It argues that these help Rwanda clean up its global image, while the conflict continues in eastern DR Congo.

items.content:
The French blood service said the attacks had occurred overnight on Monday. Photograph: Burger/Phanie/Rex/Shutterstock
The French blood service said the attacks had occurred overnight on Monday. Photograph: Burger/Phanie/Rex/Shutterstock
French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe
Temperature and defrosting thresholds raised to ‘very high levels’ at three cold stores stocking vital blood products
France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products, in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe .
The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack, adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.
The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.
The attack, which EFS said had occurred overnight on Monday, came as the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in almost a dozen European countries soared as high as 50C (122F), causing millions of euros of food damage.
Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
Retailers in Italy, Germany, Romania and the UK were targeted on Tuesday, after Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems the previous day.
In a wave of attacks in France last month, hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets. A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank said on Wednesday it had been the victim of a cyber-attack.
Something similar may have happened in the US in early August, when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries in at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.
Why are fridges being hacked and what could be next? - The Latest
After Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence officials on Tuesday, Thomas Regnier, an EU spokesperson, said the bloc’s agencies were holding urgent discussions with national authorities to formulate a collective response.
“These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said, declining to name any potential culprits. No motive for the attacks is known and no one has claimed responsibility.
A growing range of devices, including commercial refrigeration systems, can be monitored and controlled remotely. Without patching to repair emerging vulnerabilities, internet-connected software can leave code open to hackers.
Some authorities and experts fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in the aftermath of Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Western intelligence officials say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that is taking many forms.
Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos, told the Guardian this week the most plausible attribution scenarios were a “state-based signalling and demonstration of capability” or a lone-wolf hacker.
EFS said it was not directly targeted, with the attacks hitting cold stores run by its contractors. Products stored in the affected rooms, which included plasma bags for transfusions and medicine manufacturing, had been moved to other sites.
It added that France’s national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI) and the health ministry had been alerted, and monitoring of all its equipment had been reinforced.

items.title: Stock Market Today: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow Jones jump after Democratic election win - Beinsure
items.summary: Stock Market Today: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow Jones jump after Democratic election win  Beinsure
items.content:
Stock Market Today: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow Jones jump after Democratic election win
Goldman Sachs sees potential changes to tariffs and government spending
Citi warns AI infrastructure stocks could face further pressure
Wells Fargo expects economic fundamentals to outweigh politics
US manufacturing and logistics data support corporate earnings
Healthcare, renewable energy and consumer stocks lead gains
Stock market forecast: Can the rally continue through November?
US stocks rallied sharply after Democrats secured majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, prompting investors to reassess the outlook for trade policy, government spending, interest rates and artificial intelligence investment.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 1,203 points, or 2.3%, to 52,989.79 by 9:46 a.m. ET. The S&P 500 gained 1.72% to 7,698.80, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 2.13% to 25,912.39.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 1,200 points on November 4 after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, reducing political uncertainty.
Goldman Sachs expects the election outcome to influence tariffs, federal spending and the Iran conflict, while Morgan Stanley maintains an S&P 500 year-end target of 8,000.
Technology stocks rebounded, but semiconductor and AI infrastructure companies remained under pressure as investors assessed potential restrictions on data center construction.
The rebound followed a volatile October marked by concerns about AI infrastructure spending, rising corporate borrowing, elevated oil prices and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy.
Financial markets initially reacted negatively to the Democratic election victory before reversing direction as President Donald Trump indicated that he would accept the results and work with the opposition.
Investors increasingly viewed divided government as a potential constraint on further tariff increases, major fiscal changes and other policies that have contributed to market volatility. Nasdaq forecast today : Tech stocks rally after Wall Street reassesses AI spending and regulation.
The rally was broad, although gains were concentrated in large technology companies, consumer businesses and healthcare stocks. Semiconductor manufacturers and data center operators faced a different outlook as the election raised questions about future AI infrastructure development.
Goldman Sachs sees potential changes to tariffs and government spending
Goldman Sachs economists expect the Democratic takeover of Congress to give lawmakers greater influence over fiscal negotiations, trade policy and the administration's handling of the Iran conflict.
Chief economist Jan Hatzius indicated that larger Democratic majorities could strengthen the party's negotiating position while reducing the influence of smaller factions within Congress.
Goldman Sachs expects Democrats to use upcoming fiscal deadlines to seek concessions on selected tariffs, federal spending cuts and the military conflict with Iran.
The bank estimates that reversing parts of last year's spending reductions could increase federal expenditure by approximately 0.25% of GDP in 2027.
Additional agreements on healthcare subsidies or discretionary spending could provide further fiscal support. However, Goldman Sachs does not expect a major overhaul of federal AI regulation in the near term.
President Trump's veto authority and the absence of a filibuster-proof Democratic majority in the Senate limit the scope for sweeping legislative changes.
For equity markets, the immediate implication is a lower probability of abrupt changes to corporate taxation and federal spending.
The next significant fiscal deadline is December 11, when existing government funding authority expires.
Morgan Stanley remains constructive on US equities despite October's correction and persistent concerns about AI valuations. The S&P 500 rallied as investors reassessed US political risks following the Democratic victory in the midterm congressional elections.
The bank's equity strategists maintain a base-case S&P 500 target of 8,000 by the end of 2026. From the index's November 4 morning level of 7,698.80, that would represent approximately 3.9% additional upside.
Morgan Stanley identifies three issues that have constrained the market:
Uncertainty surrounding AI infrastructure investment and opposition to data center construction.
Political risks associated with the midterm elections.
Tight financial conditions, including elevated Treasury yields and restrictive monetary policy.
The election has removed one of those uncertainties, but the remaining risks have not disappeared.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management argues that markets generally respond favorably to divided government because it limits the ability of either political party to implement major changes without negotiation. He also considers a possible reduction in oil prices important for the inflation outlook.
A resolution of the Iran conflict could relieve pressure on energy costs and reduce the need for additional Federal Reserve tightening.
Morgan Stanley's economists currently expect fewer interest rate increases than financial markets have priced in, although persistent inflation could change that assessment.
The bank also expects AI investment to become more selective. Rather than concentrating exclusively on semiconductor manufacturers, future spending could increasingly benefit companies involved in electricity generation, power grids, cooling equipment and data center infrastructure.
Citi warns AI infrastructure stocks could face further pressure
The strongest divergence in Wednesday's trading emerged within the technology sector.
Amazon gained approximately 7%, Alphabet advanced more than 3%, and Microsoft and Apple also recorded substantial increases. However, companies directly exposed to AI data center construction experienced renewed selling pressure.
Citi Research's head of US equity strategy, Scott Chornert, views the election as an important reduction in political uncertainty but warns that AI infrastructure companies face additional regulatory risks.
Democratic victories in Texas and other major data center markets have increased the likelihood of restrictions on new facilities.
Dow Jones forecast : Dow surges 1,200 points as Wall Street bets on political gridlock.
Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction, citing concerns about electricity costs, water consumption and pressure on local infrastructure.
Such measures could slow investment in computing equipment, power generation and networking infrastructure.
Amazon , Alphabet and Microsoft have faced increasing scrutiny over the hundreds of billions of dollars committed to AI infrastructure.
Slower construction could reduce near-term capital expenditure and improve free cash flow, supporting valuations.
For semiconductor suppliers, however, delayed projects could translate into weaker orders and slower earnings growth.
Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron traded under pressure on Wednesday despite gains across the broader technology market.
AMD proved an exception after reporting third-quarter revenue of $13.3 bn and issuing stronger-than-expected guidance. Its shares gained approximately 5% during early trading.
The divergence suggests investors are becoming more selective about which companies will benefit financially from AI investment.
Wells Fargo expects economic fundamentals to outweigh politics
Wells Fargo Investment Institute expects the composition of Congress to influence fiscal negotiations, tariffs, defense spending and renewable energy policy.
Nevertheless, its analysis emphasizes that corporate earnings, interest rates, energy prices and consumer demand are likely to remain more important for overall market performance.
The bank does not expect sweeping policy changes under divided government. Instead, negotiations over federal borrowing and spending could determine the direction of longer-term Treasury yields. This distinction matters because the US government is already facing substantial financing requirements.
Additional fiscal expenditure may support economic growth but could also increase Treasury issuance, keeping borrowing costs elevated.
The 10-year Treasury yield declined toward 4.9% on Wednesday as investors reassessed inflation risks and the possibility of lower oil prices.
A sustained decline in bond yields would support equity valuations, particularly among companies whose expected earnings are concentrated further into the future.
However, renewed fiscal concerns or stronger-than-expected inflation could reverse that improvement.
Tesla and SpaceX shares fell sharply on November 4, 2026, after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress and secured major victories in Texas, where Elon Musk has concentrated much of his business and political activity.
US manufacturing and logistics data support corporate earnings
Recent economic indicators suggest US demand remains resilient despite elevated borrowing costs. Factory orders increased 1.8% in September, exceeding economists' expectations for a 1.2% increase. Orders were 7.2% higher than a year earlier, while demand for machinery and other capital equipment also strengthened.
Civilian aircraft orders contributed significantly to the monthly increase, meaning the headline figure should not be interpreted as evidence of equally strong growth across every manufacturing industry.
The October Logistics Managers' Index rose to 70.7 from 70.2 in September, indicating particularly strong activity across transportation, warehousing and inventory management.
Businesses continued building inventories ahead of the holiday shopping season. These figures support the earnings outlook for industrial manufacturers, logistics providers and consumer-facing companies.
However, the same report showed inventory costs rising sharply, with the relevant index reaching 88.8, its highest level since March 2022. Higher warehouse and transportation costs could eventually affect corporate profit margins.
The combination of stronger demand and persistent cost inflation complicates the Federal Reserve's decision-making.
For stocks, continued economic expansion is positive only to the extent that it does not require substantially higher interest rates.
Healthcare, renewable energy and consumer stocks lead gains
Wednesday's rally extended beyond technology. Healthcare companies benefited from expectations that Democrats could seek to reverse cuts to federal healthcare programs and expand insurance subsidies.
Molina Healthcare and Centene gained approximately 5%, while HCA Healthcare advanced around 7%.
Renewable energy stocks also strengthened as investors anticipated a more favorable environment for clean energy incentives. The Invesco Solar ETF rose approximately 8%.
Consumer companies benefited from expectations of lower energy costs and reduced trade uncertainty.
Walmart advanced around 3%, while Bank of America gained approximately 2.5%. McDonald's shares also increased following better-than-expected quarterly earnings. The company reported adjusted earnings of $3.57 per share and revenue of $7.16 bn. Although revenue missed expectations, global systemwide sales increased 4% and consolidated operating income rose 7%.
Defense contractors moved in the opposite direction. Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin declined more than 4% as investors considered the possibility of greater congressional scrutiny of defense expenditure and a diplomatic resolution to the Iran conflict.
Oil markets provided another important source of support for US equities.
West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell approximately 3% toward $93 per barrel, while Brent also declined as investors considered the possibility of renewed diplomatic negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
Lower energy prices could reduce transportation costs, ease consumer inflation and improve profit margins for airlines, retailers and industrial companies. They could also influence expectations for Federal Reserve policy.
Goldman Sachs has previously argued that an easing of the Middle East conflict could reduce the need for additional monetary tightening.
However, crude oil remains highly volatile, and a durable decline would depend on improvements in regional security and energy supply. The movement in oil prices is therefore a significant variable for the stock market's November outlook.
Stock market forecast: Can the rally continue through November?
Wednesday's advance has improved the short-term outlook, but investment bank research suggests that the sustainability of the rally will depend on earnings, inflation and financial conditions.
Morgan Stanley's 8,000 target for the S&P 500 remains achievable if corporate earnings expectations stabilize and Treasury yields decline.
Goldman Sachs sees potential support from changes to trade and fiscal policy, although the benefits would depend on negotiations between Congress and the White House.
Wells Fargo emphasizes that economic performance should ultimately have a greater influence on equity returns than the election outcome itself.
Citi's analysis highlights a more immediate risk: tighter restrictions on data center construction could produce further weakness in AI infrastructure stocks even while the broader market advances.
For November, three developments will be particularly important.
The US employment report scheduled for November 6 will provide another indication of labor market conditions.
Strong employment and wage growth could reinforce expectations that the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy.
Weaker figures could reduce pressure on interest rates but also raise concerns about slowing economic activity.
Investors will continue examining whether AI infrastructure spending is producing sufficient revenue and cash flow.
Strong results from individual technology companies may not be enough to support the entire sector if financing costs remain elevated or large projects face delays.
A sustained decline in crude oil could improve inflation expectations and support consumer spending.
Renewed escalation in the Middle East would create the opposite effect, potentially pushing energy prices and Treasury yields higher.
Historical performance offers some encouragement but little certainty.
US equities have generally delivered positive returns following midterm elections, yet the market's 2018 experience illustrates the risks of extrapolating from the initial rally. Stocks rose immediately after that election before entering a substantial correction as monetary conditions tightened.
The current market faces similar concerns about borrowing costs, alongside additional uncertainty surrounding AI investment.
The November 4 rally has reduced the political risk premium and restored demand for major US equities. Whether it becomes a sustained recovery will depend on earnings growth, lower inflation and the ability of corporate balance sheets to absorb the costs of continued investment.
