Chinese exporters see respite as Beijing curbs yuan rise amid looming record surplus
The central bank’s move to slow the yuan’s offers a breather to exporters, they say
The People’s Bank of China’s (PBOC) intervention to raise the foreign exchange reserve requirement ratio amid the yuan’s sustained rally has delivered a reprieve for China’s broader export sector, as the measure is expected to partly ease appreciation momentum driven by the country’s enormous trade surplus, analysts say.
China’s goods trade surplus mounted to a record US$938.1 billion in the January-September period , rising from US$726.2 billion in the same period a year prior. With the full year trade surplus widely expected to be higher than last year’s US$1.2 trillion record, a larger surplus brings higher foreign exchange settlement volumes.
A feedback loop – strengthening appreciation expectations, concentrated foreign exchange settlement by exporters and accelerated renminbi gains – was taking hold prior to the new PBOC policy, according to a Tuesday research note by Citic Securities in Beijing.

AMD Takes $1 Billion Hit From OpenAI and Meta AI Chip Deals
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) recorded a $1.1 billion noncash charge in the third quarter as it began accounting for stock warrants granted to OpenAI and Meta Platforms (META).
The adjustment was reflected in GAAP diluted earnings of $1.46 per share. Chief Financial Officer Jean Hu attributed it mainly to AMD's higher share price and revised estimates of whether warrant conditions will be met.
The warrants accompany chip-supply agreements with the two AI companies and could eventually let them purchase as much as 10% of AMD, subject to performance milestones. The accounting impact emerged as shipments under the arrangements began during the quarter.
Hu expects quarterly fair-value adjustments to increase in subsequent quarters as AMD ships MI450-series graphics processors and the agreements advance. The noncash changes will not affect non-GAAP earnings or free cash flow, she said.
If exercised, the warrants could dilute existing shareholders by increasing AMD's share count. The company plans to provide further guidance in 2027 on when vesting and exercise requirements may be reached, Hu said.

Historically, stocks have often performed well following midterm elections as investors gain greater clarity on the political landscape. The prospect of a divided Congress could also reduce the likelihood of major changes to fiscal and regulatory policies, providing businesses with a more predictable operating environment. However, political gridlock does not eliminate the economic challenges facing investors.
Beyond the elections, the broader outlook remains mixed. Lower energy prices and borrowing costs could provide relief to consumers and businesses, while recent corporate earnings suggest that demand remains resilient in several sectors. Nevertheless, persistent inflation, concerns surrounding artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, and uncertainty over future Federal Reserve policy remain important risks.
For investors, Wednesday's rally is encouraging, but one strong session doesn't necessarily signal the beginning of a sustained advance. The next test will be whether improving market sentiment is supported by corporate earnings, economic growth, and continued stability in financial markets.

Share Presidential hopeful Vance appears to question Iran war after polls debacle on social media
United States Vice President JD Vance arrives on Air Force Two, Monday, November 2, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, the US [Tom Brenner/Pool via AP]
US Vice President JD Vance has blamed the war on Iran for his party’s withering midterms defeat, suggesting that the conflict may not have been worth ceding control of the United States Congress to Democrats.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
Mark Pfeifle, who served as deputy national security adviser under President George W Bush, told Al Jazeera that Vance was owning up to a political failure of the administration’s own making.
“If you mess up, fess up!” he said, saying Vance was speaking up to convey that “my name was on the ballot two years ago. I have to take responsibility for this”, in a sign of political maturity and readiness to tackle Republicans’ biggest political liabilities.
US Vice President JD Vance speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Swanton, Ohio on November 2, 2026 [AFP] MAGA heir
Vance, a likely 2028 presidential candidate and heir apparent to US President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, has been a key negotiator as the US and Iran search for a way out of the eight-month conflict, which has dented their economies and pushed global fuel prices up.
His statements on Tehran have been more dovish than those of other key members of the administration, and his post-election note appears to mark the closest he has yet come to publicly diverging from Trump on an issue that looks set to dog Republicans as the war continues.
“Vance is definitely trying to distance himself from Trump, as many other respectable Republicans will do over the next several weeks and months,” said Nick Rahall, a former Democratic member of Congress. “The people have spoken.”
“It had even leaked before that JD was the only one in Trump’s inner circle who had questions and was hesitant about Iran [war] from the beginning,” Rahall added.
Citing a pollster he describes as “one of the smartest people I know”, Vance said he was told ending the Iran war and “changing our relationship with Israel” were two of the top four answers given by Americans surveyed who had voted for Trump in 2024 but were planning to vote for Democrats in the 2026 midterms.
In stark contrast, Trump said, in the wake of the rebuke at the ballot box , that he had no regrets about launching the conflict.
“I did the right thing. I would have done it again ,” he told the Wall Street Journal.

items.title: Persian Gulf leaders fear a renewed US-Iran war as diplomacy sputters - The Spokesman-Review
items.summary: Persian Gulf leaders fear a renewed US-Iran war as diplomacy sputters  The Spokesman-Review
items.content:
Iranians burn U.S. and Israel flags during a rally in front of the former U.S. embassy to mark the anniversary of the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, in Tehran, Iran, on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. In 1979, 52 embassy staff were held hostage for 444 days by Iranian students, who demanded that Washington hand over Iran's recently toppled shah, who was being treated in the United States for cancer.  (ATTA KENARE/AFP/Getty Images North America/ / Tribune News Service)
MANAMA, Bahrain — Conferences in the Persian Gulf are usually positive affairs, with government officials, executives of state-owned companies and armies of consultants touting petro-fueled visions promising fantastical technology and prosperity.
Yet optimism seemed in short supply at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security and geopolitical summit held in the Bahraini capital. Instead, the dominant mood among the Middle East diplomats, defense officials and experts assembled last weekend was fear over the consequences of another bout of U.S.-Iran fighting.
“The rules of logic tell us that the Iranian stand and the American stand are far apart. And if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” Anwar Gargash, a presidential advisor in the United Arab Emirates, said in an address at the summit.
Gargash added that it’s not in the interest of the regional countries or Iran to go through another round of war.
“While we’re going through this period of protracted crisis of no war, no peace, we are clearly seeking a political offramp,” he said.
In his address, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said, “We have to push very hard in order to prevent the escalation.”
Noting that more fighting would affect food and energy security, he added, “The second round will be more dangerous, more destructive and it will lead to nowhere.”
With a settlement between Tehran and Washington seemingly out of reach, President Trump has hinted he could launch “another little Operation Epic Fury” after Tuesday’s midterm elections. He was referring to the U.S.-Israeli operation that launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28.
But on Monday, he wrote on his social media website that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”
Still, hours later, Iranian state media reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz; the Associated Press quoted an unnamed U.S. official as saying the military had carried out “defensive strikes.”
The news comes as Republicans face a tough midterm race, which has become a referendum on an increasingly unpopular war that could sink Trump’s Teflon-like electoral appeal.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political life after an inconclusive election last month, is said to be pressing Trump to finish off the Islamic Republic.
Behind the scenes, regional diplomats are engaging in furious shuttle diplomacy to avert renewed fighting. Last week, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials flew to Tehran and met with Iranian military officials. Qatar is leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, with Tehran presenting a de-escalation plan that has yet to be accepted by Trump.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Monday told the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency that it was now up to the Americans to decide “whether they have the will to take the wise path of diplomacy or, as in the past, seek to drag the situation into aggression and military operations.”
“If they dare to test us again,” he added, “they know that they will receive a much more bitter and severe result than before.”
His words came as several Middle Eastern countries are still reeling from the first round of fighting, when Iran retaliated against U.S. attacks by striking American military bases on regional soil with fusillades of drones, as well as cruise and ballistic missiles.
Iran also targeted civilian infrastructure and has vowed to exercise less restraint and wage a no-holds-barred campaign — possibly striking energy, desalination and travel facilities — in the event of a new assault.
On Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said further U.S. attacks would prompt a broad response, one without “geographic limits.”
The scars of the fight could be seen around the Bahraini capital, where the U.S. 5th Fleet has several support facilities. Structures showed signs of explosive damage, including a partially destroyed radar dish and soot-covered depot, a result of Iranian projectiles — 500 drones and roughly 200 ballistic missiles — finding their mark.
The bases seemed all but abandoned, with word among residents that American service members, a common sight in Bahrain, have all but disappeared.
The war has cast a shadow on Persian Gulf nations that have long presented themselves as paragons of stability in a volatile region, mostly unaffected by the conflicts raging in the wider Middle East.
Disruptions to energy flows and logistics mean members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, or GCC, a bloc of oil-rich Gulf nations, are facing a 4.8% contraction in gross domestic product compared with last year, according to the International Monetary Fund.
The International Monetary Fund expected a strong turnaround in 2027 but acknowledged that “uncertainty remains exceptionally high, and risks are firmly tilted to the downside.”
Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are hardest hit; Qatar’s real GDP is down more than 15% this year. Meanwhile, the Saudi economy — which is contending with the double pressures of a sealed-off Strait of Hormuz and a blockade on Red Sea access by Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, shrank almost 4% in the third quarter compared with last year, according to official figures.
Despite regional efforts to bring about a detente, the general consensus among attendees at the security summit was that more war is coming. The summit, which is organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies think tank, drew hundreds of participants.
And for both regional and European officials present, there was a deep sense of uncertainty regarding Washington and its commitment to shielding putative allies from attack.
That has forced Gulf nations — long reliant on a U.S. security umbrella — to look for protection beyond Washington. Yet diplomats lamented what they said was a lack of coordination close to home, despite a long-standing GCC mutual defense agreement.
For example, militaries detecting projectiles in their airspace that were en route to a target country didn’t warn their counterparts, leaving them with less time to deal with incoming attacks. Others have systems that are not linked to the U.S.’s regional radar net.
“A lot of countries you thought you can depend on were not there for you,” Gargash said. “Why did we sign that agreement many years ago only to see that this agreement was not activated when we all needed it?”
Saudi Arabia has sought to marshal alternative allies through a recently signed pact with Turkey and Pakistan, and has asked Egypt for help — a request Cairo said it would honor by engaging in defensive operations on Saudi territory.
But Abdelatty, Egypt’s foreign minister, said the region requires more than new military engagements and should instead “move from the logic of crisis management to the logic of building an order” aimed at stopping confrontations before they start.
“A war can begin with a unilateral decision,” Abdelatty said.
“But no one can unilaterally control its consequences or stop it.”

Conventional wisdom holds that foreign policy doesn’t affect the outcome of American elections, but it cratered President Donald Trump’s party in this one, at least indirectly. High prices, which swelled the magnitude of the “blue tsunami,” were clearly the result of Trump’s tariffs and his war on Iran.
One question now is whether the Democrats will be able to use their overwhelming majorities in the House and Senate to push back on those policies.
Trump will probably resist the effort, claiming his powers, under Article 2 of the Constitution, as the armed forces’ commander in chief. He also threatened to veto bills that he considers “ insane ,” a term he applies to anything that challenges his prerogatives and priorities.
But a few caveats are worth noting. First, Democrats are projected to win at least 250 of the 435 seats in the House—just 40 seats short of the two-thirds needed to override a presidential veto. And given the widespread unpopularity of Trump’s war, tariffs, and other unilateral aggressions, it may not be so difficult to rally 40 Republicans to join an override campaign.
A huge consequence of the Democrats’ victory—especially its scale and margin, even in states that had previously been seen as Republican sure things—is the evaporation of Trump’s biggest reservoir of power: the fear that kept the entire GOP in his thrall. After the defeat of so many candidates handpicked by Trump, his threat to throw primary challengers against disloyal party members no longer carries much weight.
It is worth noting that the Vietnam War was ended in 1973 by a congressional amendment that cut off funding for any combat activities in the region. It’s also worth noting that the Senate at first narrowly defeated the measure but then passed it overwhelmingly a year later, after the 1972 elections—which widened the Democrats’ majority by two seats—and the deepening revulsion toward President Richard Nixon amid the Watergate scandal.
The language of the bill, sponsored in the Senate by Republican Clifford Case and Democrat Frank Church, was very specific:
None of the funds herein appropriated under this Act may be expended to support directly or indirectly combat activities in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam and South Vietnam or off the shores of Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam and South Vietnam by United States forces, and after August 15, 1973, no other funds heretofore appropriate under any other act may be expended for such purpose.
Nearly identical language could be drafted this January, with a good chance of success, substituting the names of Iran and various other Middle Eastern countries.
It’s also quite possible that the boundless supply of U.S. weapons to Israel—a nearly automatic reflex for decades—will soon be sharply restricted, if not cut off entirely. Even Trump has said that he would soon end military aid to Israel, though he didn’t foreclose the option of selling Israel arms that the country needed. (The fact that he said this the day before the election, as a last-minute appeal to voters, illustrates just how Israel’s star has fallen.)
Meanwhile, Trump’s $1.5 trillion defense budget —a near–50 percent increase over the previous year’s allotment—is dead on arrival. (Signs of impending demise were flashing even before the election.) There will be pressure to boost some line items, in order to replace the vast stocks of U.S. munitions depleted and aircraft destroyed in the Iran war. Some will propose filling these gaps by cutting some of Trump’s cherished projects—the Golden Dome (which will cost hundreds of billions of dollars and still not provide defense) and the new fleet of battleships (which the Navy didn’t request and doesn’t want).
Back in 2021, after Joe Biden ended Trump’s first term as president, Rep. Adam Smith , the then-new chairman of the Armed Services Committee, talked about “smart” ways to cut the defense budget, which at the time totaled $750 billion, by $100 billion. (Vladimir Putin’s aggression in Ukraine soon snapped those visions.) This January, Smith will regain the chair. Have he and his staff worked up a way to cut $500 billion from the current bloat?
To put it another way: Will the Democratic Congress revive the sort of defense analysis that its committees once performed (to some degree), weighing the costs and benefits of various programs in the context of military missions and strategies? Or will it drop the ball, as recent Congresses have routinely done, and accept just about everything that the top generals and admirals request but freeze the budget’s size—neither boosting some programs nor slashing others, thus satisfying nobody?
Whatever approach the Democrats take, the results of the midterms—the strong support for social programs and the broad opposition to the war in Iran—take a sizable defense-budget increase (or possibly any increase at all) off the table.
At the same time, few Democrats in Congress are isolationists. They tend to support strengthened sanctions against Russia, vigorous support for Ukraine, and a friendly attitude toward allies—if just because Trump has taken the opposite stance on all three. It will be interesting to see how they reconcile these positions with fiscal priorities.
Meanwhile, the Democrats are no doubt considering a more urgent Pentagon reform—getting rid of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Back in September, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, canvassed wide bipartisan support for an eight-point resolution of impeachment against Hegseth. House Speaker Mike Johnson ended the session , weeks ahead of schedule, in part to prevent the measure from coming up.
Massie said on Monday that he would reintroduce the bill after the midterms if Hegseth hasn’t been fired in the meantime .* Hakeem Jeffries, who will most likely be elected the new speaker in January, chimed in that Congress would run Hegseth “out of town” if the Democrats took the majority. The Hill reported earlier this week that Senate Democrats have floated the idea of demanding Hegseth’s ouster as the price for passing any of Trump’s defense programs.
Trump continues to tout Hegseth as a “ great warrior .” But Trump has been known to throw even the most loyal of aides under the bus if it serves his own interests. As the electoral losses piled up Tuesday night, Trump allowed in a Wall Street Journal interview that the war “ was a piece of it .” The morning after, Vice President J.D. Vance went further, posting on social media, “The reason we lost is the war [and] everyone knows” it, adding, “The president himself said so last night.”
Vance’s post might be seen as his opening bid to run for president in 2028—dissociating himself from Trump’s most disastrous policy but not from Trump. It’s a fine tightrope to navigate.
What Trump does with Hegseth depends in part on what he wants to do in Iran. If he resumes bombing, as he said he might do after the midterms , then Hegseth provides useful cover. If he decides not to restart the war, as he also signaled might be the case a few days before the election , then Trump needs someone to blame for what he would now acknowledge is a mistake. Donald J. Trump doesn’t admit making mistakes. So Hegseth would take the fall.
Correction, Nov. 4, 2026: This article originally misstated that Massie said he would reintroduce the impeachment resolution against Hegseth during next year’s congressional session. He stated that he would reintroduce the resolution after the midterms.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has said that anyone expecting a shift in the United States’ policy towards his country is “seriously mistaken”, hours after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.
“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Khamenei said in a written statement published on his website.

Iran’s head of state, who has not appeared publicly since his father and predecessor Ali Khamenei was assassinated in a US-Israeli attack on his office in February, said Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz had shattered the “myth of America’s invincibility” and warned that any renewed US attack would draw a far wider response .
Khamenei’s statement came on the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, which Iran marks each year as the “National Day of the Fight Against Global Arrogance”.
“In the event of repeated transgression, it will take on much wider dimensions,” he said, warning that any renewed US attacks on Iran could lead to a wider conflict.
Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran that began in February likely impacted his Republican Party’s poor performance in the elections, but argued that voters were reacting to higher petrol prices rather than the military campaign itself.
“I don’t think it’s the war,” he told Fox News on Tuesday. “I think it’s the gasoline prices.”
“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequences of paying more for gasoline.”
Trump also left open the possibility of a major new attack on Iran, telling the Fox & Friends programme on Tuesday that some people were pushing for what he described as a “heavy hit”.
“A lot of people would like to do the heavy hit. A lot of people wouldn’t,” he said.
Khamenei’s comments came as another top Iranian official struck a more conciliatory tone on Wednesday following the results of the US vote, which saw Democrats score a historic victory by taking control of both chambers of Congress.
“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” said Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator with Washington and his country’s parliament speaker.
“If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added on X.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser and assistant to the supreme leader, said Trump had been “slapped in the face by his own people”.
“The true winner in this arena was Iran, which transferred the cost of the war into the United States,” he wrote on X.
A banner with a picture of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei during the 47th anniversary of the US expulsion from Iran, in Tehran, November 4, 2026 [Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via Reuters] ‘Pure revenge’
But Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, warned that the Democrats’ victory could actually increase the risk of Trump escalating in the short term.
”He has shown a pattern in which, in face of humiliation and defeat, he becomes more reckless,” he said, adding that Trump could respond to the election by ramping up attacks against Iran out of “pure revenge”.
Parsi warned that the period between now and January, before Democrats take control of Congress, could be particularly volatile, as that’s when Democrats could try to use their new majority to restrict funding for the war.
“The combination of him running out of time and him becoming more reckless as a result of a defeat creates a very dangerous period for the next two months,” he said.
The US has warned it could carry out a short but intensive military campaign against Iran after the midterms.
Hamidreza Moghadamfar, an adviser to the commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Iran would hit targets beyond US bases if Gulf states allowed Washington to launch attacks from their territory. Speaking at a rally in Bandar Abbas, he named the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain and said Iran would respond with a “new doctrine and new technology”.
Trump said the US was prepared to act, but suggested another attack might not be necessary as hopes for a negotiated solution linger.
“I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” he said in an interview with the Financial Times.

The death of physical games could be getting closer as Macronix, one of Nintendo's key ROM chip suppliers for Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges, is reportedly shutting down its ROM business to focus on manufacturing NOR and NAND flash chips to supply data centers, multiple reports claim. Storage is already becoming expensive, and Macronix's move may force Nintendo to increase cartridge prices, produce more Game-Key cards, or lean more towards digital purchases.
AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply
Samsung debuts three next-generation memory technologies for AI data centers
"Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch business," MST Financial David Gibson reports on X. "Macronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately.
1/4 Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch business
Macronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately. November 4, 2026
He notes that Macronix ROM sales in Q3 of this year dropped to 5%, compared to last year's 26%. Furthermore, Gibson says that the NT$37.8 billion capital expenditure is allocated to NOR and NAND Flash, leaving none for ROM as the company shifts its manufacturing capacity to supply AI needs — Taipei Times corroborated the report, stating, "At the same time, Macronix is gradually phasing out of ROM production, Wu said. It also reports that Macronix's capital expenditure is split into two phases, the NT$ 22 billion for expanding manufacturing capacity, followed by an additional NT$15.8 billion for NAND flash used in eMMCs and 3D NAND.
Gibson expects that Nintendo's digital margins will grow through more Game-Key Cards or digital-only sales, but as Macronix isn't the only source of ROM chips, "physical cards will likely carry on for some time." Gibson further reports that digital margins have been slowly rising, with numbers fluctuating depending on the quarter due to major physical game launches.
3/4 My view: Macronix isn't Nintendo's only game memory card maker, so physical cards will likely carry on for some time. But at the margin, digital will grow, through more Game-Key Cards (which hold a download key, not the game) and digital-only sales. November 4, 2026
ROHM group companies ROHM Semiconductor and LAPIS Semiconductor still supply ROM chips to Nintendo, so it's unlikely that Nintendo will eventually go digital-only in the near future like Sony and Microsoft 's recent plans. With one less supplier, however, Nintendo may be forced to increase prices on physical games.
The biggest loser in all of this (besides the gamers), however, may be fabless chip design company MegaChips. Nintendo doesn't buy ROM chips from Macronix directly; MegaChips designs the ROM chips according to Nintendo's needs and, having no manufacturing capacity, outsources it to Macronix. MegaChips' 2022 company report states that Nintendo accounted for 87.8% of its sales, while Macronix accounted for 67.8% of its outsourced manufacturing purchases. The report even states that if Macronix could manufacture ROM chips, "MegaChips' operating results may be impacted." The 2022 document further says that there was no sign that the risk would become apparent; however, the risk just became very real, and we're not aware of MegaChips' contingency plan to deal with this situation. However, Macronix and MegaChips have likely talked amongst themselves about Macronix's plans to stop ROM chip manufacturing, and have given MegaChips some time to find another manufacturer before Macronix shuts down the ROM chip business.

This week, markets have been keyed into the midterms as Democrats and Republicans vie for majority control in the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Early vote counts indicated that the Democrats are headed for majority control in the House as well as the Senate as 2026 U.S. midterm elections polls are inching nearer to close.
The Kobeissi Letter said in a post on X that the Nasdaq 100 futures extended losses to nearly 1.5% on the day as the odds of a Democrat "sweep" rose to 95%, adding that the S&P 500 has now erased about $500 billion in market cap over the last 2 hours.
Prediction market Kalshi put the odds for a Democratic win of the Senate at about 90%, while odds for Democratic control of the House jumped to 97%. Meanwhile, a Stocktwits poll also indicated that markets were largely clocking a win for Democrats in the midterms. Of the roughly 19,400 voters on the poll that sought to gauge how the midterms would go, a 52% majority voted that Democrats would win both chambers.
A "blue wave" scenario is likely to put pressure on the artificial intelligence buildout as investors see a Democratic win as likely to bring in more restrictions on data centers.

items.title: 'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono
items.summary: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono puts out a statement through his club, expressing his sorrow and pain after Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel's death.
items.content:
Figure caption, Fans pay respects to Tenerife's De Miguel
By David Watkinson ,Â  BBC Sport senior journalist Â  and Â  Ffion Wynne ,Â  BBC Sport journalist
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.
The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally".
"These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement.
"I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened.
"I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him.
"I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing.
Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.
Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.
Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.
The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player.
"As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.
Image caption, Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year deal
On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.
Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.
The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.
Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".
"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.
Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

items.content:
The demand for ASML's machines has increased significantly, as they are used to manufacture advanced chips for AI applications.
TSMC is the world's largest semiconductor foundry, and it has a strong clientele that uses its advanced process nodes to make AI chips.
The semiconductor industry has experienced phenomenal growth in recent years, driven primarily by the rapid deployment of data centers capable of handling artificial intelligence (AI) workloads.
The Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) notes that the semiconductor industry generated $439 billion in revenue in 2020, up 6.5% from the prior year. That figure jumped to $792 billion in 2025, increasing by nearly 26% from 2024. McKinsey estimates that the semiconductor industry could generate a whopping $2.3 trillion in revenue in 2030, well above the $1.6 trillion guidance issued a year ago.
This is great news for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ( TSM -2.24% ) and ASML Holding ( ASML -3.60% ) , two of the most important companies in the semiconductor ecosystem. Both companies enjoy an almost monopoly like position in their respective semiconductor niches. But if you have to choose one of them for your portfolio right now, which one should it be?
TSMC and ASML sit at the top of the semiconductor supply chain
While TSMC is the world's largest semiconductor foundry, manufacturing chips for leading fabless chipmakers and consumer electronics companies, ASML makes the machines that help TSMC manufacture those chips.
ASML's extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines play a critical role in helping foundries and memory manufacturers make advanced chips based on small process nodes. These EUV machines use light to intricately print billions of transistors on a chip. The higher transistor density makes chips faster and more power-efficient, and chip designers can shrink the size of chips as well.

This explains why AI chip designers, such as Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices , Broadcom , and others, are designing chips based on process nodes that are 5-nanometer (nm) or smaller. As a result, the demand for ASML's advanced chipmaking equipment has been growing at an incredible pace. The number of new lithography systems sold by ASML jumped by 71% year over year last quarter to 113.
ASML expects robust demand for its machines to continue. It plans to increase the production capacity of EUV machines by 30% next year and aims to expand capacity by more than 30% in 2028. So, ASML's strong growth momentum seems sustainable over the long run. The company's revenue increased by 55% year over year in Q3 to 11.66 billion euros, while net income increased by 133% from the year-ago period.
Given that ASML is the only manufacturer of EUV machines capable of producing advanced AI chips, it enjoys robust pricing power. Not surprisingly, ASML could capitalize on the strong demand and limited supply of its machines by raising prices, thereby supporting its earnings growth over the long run. That's why analysts have been becoming bullish about ASML's long-term earnings growth potential.
TSMC, on the other hand, is an ASML customer. The Taiwan-based foundry giant recently said it will use ASML's High NA EUV machines to increase the production of advanced chips. Moreover, TSMC sees an increase in the adoption of ASML's High NA EUV machines to meet the growing demand for AI chips.
It is easy to see why that's the case. TSMC gets the majority of its revenue from manufacturing advanced chips for its customers. Specifically, 79% of its revenue came from chips made using the 7nm process node or below in Q3. That was an improvement over the year-ago period's contribution of 74%. So, TSMC is likely to purchase more machines from ASML in the future to support its healthy growth.
TSMC's revenue increased by 41% year over year in Q3 to $46.7 billion. Moreover, the company controls 73% of the global foundry market, according to Counterpoint Research, well ahead of the second-placed company's 7% share. This monopoly like position allows TSMC to raise prices for its advanced chip nodes, especially given solid demand and tight supply.
This is why its net profit margin increased by 5.4 percentage points year over year in the previous quarter, leading to a 69% jump in earnings per share (EPS) to $29.43. So, both ASML and TSMC are clocking solid growth rates, which they can sustain over the long run due to the secular growth opportunity in semiconductors.
In fact, just like ASML, analysts have increased their long-term growth expectations for TSMC as well.
TSMC and ASML's dominant positions in their respective niches make both worth buying right now. However, we saw in the previous section that ASML is currently clocking much faster growth, and it can sustain the same by increasing the production capacity of its advanced EUV machines.
However, investors will have to pay a premium to buy ASML over TSMC.
The good part is that ASML can justify its valuation, especially considering its triple-digit earnings growth. However, investors seeking a mix of growth and value can consider buying TSMC. After all, even TSMC is growing at a nice pace, and analysts expect its earnings per share to increase at a 40%-plus rate over the long run.
In the end, investors won't go wrong with either ASML or TSMC, and choosing one of these two AI stocks depends on how much valuation they are willing to pay to make the most of the booming semiconductor industry.

This is great news for Micron stock investors, especially given that it trades at an attractive 12 times earnings. Micron's 24% share of the dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) market and 15% share of NAND flash storage memory put it in a terrific position to sustain the healthy growth it has been clocking over the past couple of years.

Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures.
In an interview at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, asked if he was worried the results might make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham replied:
President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.
That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves.
But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. The conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.
These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that. And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do.
Some politicians and commentators have interpreted the results as evidence that rightwing populism is in retreat around the world. But when asked if he thought the elections were part of a global pattern, Burnham was reluctant to make that claim. Instead, he replied:
I think people want to see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people, and that’s what the voters, in my view, are saying in the United States.
Let’s get focused in a laser-like way on those cost of living issues. And I think around the world there’s a recognition that countries can’t do that on their own, and can’t do that when we have division between nations.
I’ve been working hard as prime minister to bring a new approach, a new approach in the Middle East, and the foreign secretary set that out [with the announcements about sanctions on illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank].
A new approach to Europe, and we believe that will help us get growth back up and reduce those cost of living pressures. But a new approach with the Commonwealth too.
Asked if Britain would be pushing for de-escalation in the Iran war, Burnham said:
I’ll be working for de-escalation. To make it very clear, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again. That’s what we will be working towards.

Burghart asked Haigh how much the government was spending on working-age welfare and, when she refused to answer, he said the figure was £183bn.

John Swinney , Scotland’s first minister, has rejected calls from MSPs for a review of laws which allow people with limited rights to live in the UK to stand for Holyrood.
Yesterday the standards, procedures and public appointments committee, chaired by the Scottish National party MSP Jenni Minto, said the reforms could undermine “fragile” confidence amongst voters in the country’s institutions.
Swinney told LBC he had no plans to review the provisions, which first came into force this year in the Scottish Elections (Representation and Reform) Act 2025. He said:
We don’t intend to do so, no. The parliament voted unanimously for the provision for foreign nationals to be able to stand for elections in certain circumstances.
The reforms came under intense scrutiny after the May election after the Conservatives and Reform UK protested about the election of Q Manivannan, an Indian citizen, for the Scottish Greens in Edinburgh and Lothians East region.
A post-graduate student at St Andrews, it emerged their student visa was due to expire at the end of 2026. They have since been granted a three-year graduate visa, given them right to remain until the end of 2029.
Swinney’s government is bidding to expand the provisions of the act by including Commonwealth citizens, who were excluded as a category last year. Swinney told LBC “the government will press ahead with that.” Manivannan only qualified because they were on a student visa, not because they were a Commonwealth citizen.
The act covers elections to Holyrood and Scottish councils; Westminster contests in Scotland are reserved to Westminster and excluded.
The Department for Work and Pensions ’ report released today on the employment of disabled people (see 2.41pm ) says that the financial year ending 2026 was the first for more than a decade where the number of disabled working-age people in the UK fell. It says it is too early to know if this was just temporary. It explains:
This (FYE [financial year ending] 2026) is the first full year since financial year ending (FYE) 2014 where the number of disabled people and disability prevalence have decreased, by 0.5% (around 50,000) and by 0.2 percentage points, respectively. It is too early to determine whether this is a temporary change, also as the latest quarterly data for April to June 2026 reports a year-on-year significant increase in the number of disabled people (250,000).
Number of working-age disabled people in UK Photograph: DWP The Commons Treasury committee has started taking evidence from officials from the Office for Budget Responsibility about the budget. Harriett Baldwin , a Conservative member of the committee, asked about Shabana Mahmood’s announcement on Monday axing some of the restrictions to indefinite leave to remain (ILR) that had been planned by the Home Office.
The Tories claim this U-turn will cost the exchequer £10bn.
Asked what impact this announcement would have on the OBR’s fiscal assumptions, Tom Josephs , a member of the OBR’s budget responsibility committee, said the OBR would have to review this for its next forecast in the spring. He said he could not give an answer now.
Asked if he thought it really would cost £10bn, Josephs said “that is not an estimate that we produced”. He said that was a government estimate for the lifetime cost of some migrants.
Asked if the change on Monday would be "material enough” to require a change to the OBR’s forecast, Josephs just said the OBR would assess the policy as a whole. “If we think [the Monday announcement is] significant enough to adjust the forecast, then we will do so.”
Mahmood originally produced the £10bn figure to justify the plans she originally announced last year. She said making it harder for migrant workers to get ILR would save the government £10bn over time.
This claim backfired when Mahmood U-turned on a large part of her plan, leading the Tories to claim she was now in effect raising spending by almost £10bn (because the savings were forgone).
Some experts claim the £10bn figure for supposed savings was never realistic in the first place.
Just under half of young people not in work, education or training were classed as disabled in the year to March – a proportion which has more than doubled in just over a decade, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The government is currently working on reducing the number of 16 to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training – known as Neets – with a review expected to be published in the coming weeks making recommendations for changes in the system.
The number of Neets topped a million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade, fuelling calls for more help to get young people into work.
Government data published today showed 45.3% of Neets were classed as disabled in the year to March.
The Department for Work and Pensions said this was a rise of 24.2 percentage points since the proportion of 21.1% in the 12 months to March 2014.
The latest data showed disabled young people were more than three times as likely to be Neet compared to non-disabled young people – 30.2% compared with 8.6%.
Depression, bad nerves or anxiety was the most common main health condition reported by disabled Neets, accounting for almost a quarter (23.8%), followed by autism (22.7%).
Proportion of young people who are Neet who are disabled Photograph: DWP Andy Burnham has urged Poundland bosses to work with the government on trying to find a “practical solution” to the problems that have left the company on the brink of administration.
In a pooled interview, asked if he had a message for Poundland executives, Burnham replied:
Focus on the people in your employment, meet with the business secretary because we are setting up that meeting, come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores because many of them are viable propositions, they’re on high streets, they matter in our communities. There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let’s find it.
When it was put to him that there was a limit to what the government could do if the company was not profitable, he replied:
There’s always a limit, but we’re prepared to find what we can do. We believe in this instance there is a solution. There are many viable outlets here. Other retailers are expressing interest. Get around the table. Let’s find a solution.
Andy Burnham in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, today. Photograph: Kin Cheung/AP Here is an initial take from Pippa Crerar , the Guardian’s political editor, on what the US election results might mean for the UK.
While the public here in the UK - which overwhelmingly believes his presidency has been bad for Britain - may welcome the ‘blue tsunami’, ministers and officials will be watching nervously for how Trump reacts.
The US president acknowledged overnight the Iran conflict - which has pushed up the cost of living globally - had cost the Republicans votes and has previously suggested a deal could be struck with Tehran post-midterms.
But there are concerns here that a bruised Trump - whose domestic agenda is constrained after losing control of Congress but who still wields a veto and significant power over foreign policy - could now lash out like a caged animal.
There could be a backlash on the world stage as he tries to cement his legacy during his last two years, potentially including more military action in Iran, Ukraine and even Cuba; more trade tariffs; and more unhelpful interventions in UK and European politics.
But for now, there is also relief that the US has cast its verdict on Trump and his combative style of politics, and hope that if the Democrats get their act together (for this was a referendum on the US president rather than a ringing endorsement of his opponents), the 2028 election could transform the special relationship.
Andy Burnham has said that he hopes the sweeping losses for Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US elections will give the world an “opportunity” to focus on ending the Iran war and easing the cost of living pressures.
In an interview at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua, asked if he was worried the results might make Trump more unpredictable, Burnham replied:
President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living.
That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we’ve made moves.
But I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. The conflict in Ukraine started by Russia.
These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that. And certainly, in my calls with leaders, that is what I will be asking everybody to do.
Some politicians and commentators have interpreted the results as evidence that rightwing populism is in retreat around the world. But when asked if he thought the elections were part of a global pattern, Burnham was reluctant to make that claim. Instead, he replied:
I think people want to see the world coming together and focusing on the things that matter to people, and that’s what the voters, in my view, are saying in the United States.
Let’s get focused in a laser-like way on those cost of living issues. And I think around the world there’s a recognition that countries can’t do that on their own, and can’t do that when we have division between nations.
I’ve been working hard as prime minister to bring a new approach, a new approach in the Middle East, and the foreign secretary set that out [with the announcements about sanctions on illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank].
A new approach to Europe, and we believe that will help us get growth back up and reduce those cost of living pressures. But a new approach with the Commonwealth too.
Asked if Britain would be pushing for de-escalation in the Iran war, Burnham said:
I’ll be working for de-escalation. To make it very clear, we want to see a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz fully opened again. That’s what we will be working towards.
Andy Burnham being interviewed by the BBC’s Chris Mason in St. John's, Antigua. Photograph: Kin Cheung/PA If you are deputising at PMQs, it may be nice to get a good write-up from the sketchwriters, and satisfying to craft a line that will play well on the TV or radio later, but, frankly, one task matters above all others: don’t mess up. And, in that respect, Louise Haigh and Alex Burghart both performed well – in exchanges likely to be quickly forgotten.
For Haigh, this was her first time, but it did not particularly sound like this. She sounded confident and authoritative, without being brash and hubristic. She did not have anything very new to say about welfare, and Labour does not have a firm answer yet to the question as to when it will cut the benefits bill, but Haigh swerved this quite adequately with attacks on the Tories’ record and by making the Labour argument about now wanting welfare spending on failure. She said:
We have been repeatedly clear that we cannot afford to pay for failure and must invest in success – and that is how we will bring the welfare bill down.
We will make support more conditional on taking up opportunities, ensuring young people get help they need earlier, tackling the long-term drivers of welfare spending, including high housing costs, and we will do all this in a Labour way.
She would not rule out tax rises to pay for more welfare spending (see 2.16pm ), but that was the sort of question opposition parties ask when they can’t think of a proper, specific one and so instead have to resort to simplistic politics-by-slogan.
Burghart has done PMQs before, and he was a bit more polished. His pre-scripted riffs about “two 10-year plans in 10 months”, and John Healey’s Today programme welfare gaffe last week, were elegantly done, but not quite withering or funny enough to be truly damaging. He didn’t fail, but he didn’t score.
The most interesting question came from the Lib Dem deputy leader Daisy Cooper, who is probably the first MP to get a ‘Trump might be a rapist’ allegation into Hansard. (See 12.29pm .) Rather ingeniously, she tried to suggest there might be some sort of UK government angle. But there probably isn’t. This is one for Congress.
If anyone had a bad PMQs, it was probably Lindsay Hoyle. It was not clear who he was referring to when he delivered his ‘don’t shout a woman down’ bollocking to some Tory MP. (See 12.20pm .) But it sounded a bit chauvinist. Haigh is the second most senior person in government; she seemed perfectly capable of coping with a bit of heckling; and if shouting down a minister is unacceptable, it should not matter what sex they are.
Helen Maguire (Lib Dem) asks about conditions at Epsom hospital, where urgent repairs are needed.
Haigh says she is aware of the problems. The minister is happy to meet Maguire to discuss the situation, she says.
Munira Wilson (Lib Dem) says Haigh recently said the government would give local leaders more power to invest in things that matter. But it is cutting funding for Richmond council by more than £100m over the next four years, 60% of its budget? Will Haigh meet her to discuss this to find a solution.
Haigh says the government inherited an unfair council funding system. She offers Wilson a meeting with a minister.
Bobby Dean (Lib Dem) asks if the government will back legislation to make US tech companies pay fair compensation to victims of online scams. He says, given the US election results, the government should be tougher with the US administration.
Haigh says the Online Safety Act requires tech companies to take robust action on online scams.

US Stock Market Today: S&P 500 Futures Edge Higher On Strong Factory And Freight Data
The Morning Bull - US Market Morning Update Wednesday, Nov, 4 2026
US markets are set for a cautiously positive open, with sentiment leaning risk on as investors focus on a clear growth story. The single driver today is stronger US manufacturing and logistics activity pointing to resilient demand.
Factory orders for September rose 1.8%, the firmest reading since April, led by a 4.6% jump in transportation equipment. The US Logistics Managers' Index climbed to 70.7 in October, signaling robust freight activity and fuller warehouses ahead of the holiday season.
Stronger orders and busier supply chains support expectations that revenue pipelines remain healthy, which can steady earnings projections across goods producers and transport linked businesses. Firmer demand data also shapes views on future borrowing costs, since resilient activity can influence how comfortable policymakers feel keeping financial conditions tight.
The open question is how long this strength can run before it collides with policy or cost pressures. Upcoming US labor data and wage readings later this week will test whether today's growth friendly narrative still holds or needs to be repriced.
Fresh Q3 numbers put McDonald's in focus. The chain reported earnings of US$2.49b and adjusted EPS of US$3.57, both above Wall Street expectations. Revenue of US$7.16b came in below forecasts, although global systemwide sales rose 4% and consolidated operating income increased 7%. A 4% lift in the quarterly dividend to US$1.93 signals management confidence to income focused investors.
Microsoft is back in AI headlines. The group launched the Frontier Launchpad program with NVIDIA for UK and Irish software firms that build on AI tools, offering technical and commercial support. OpenAI, in which Microsoft holds a large stake, is also acquiring Pierre Computer to deepen Codex developer tools. Readers may watch how these moves reinforce Microsoft's AI ecosystem.
Fresh results and a new roadmap put Emerson Electric on pre market watchlists. Underlying orders in the fourth quarter rose 14% and net sales grew 7% for fiscal 2026. The board lifted the quarterly cash dividend by 7%. Initial 2027 guidance calls for about 5% sales growth and adjusted EPS of roughly US$7.25, giving investors clearer earnings benchmarks.
Fiserv (FISV) jumped 12.46% after a Q3 earnings beat, a doubled cost savings target, and renewed buyback plans.
Bloom Energy (BE) climbed 9.05% on a Barclays upgrade and a California Resources partnership targeting 1 GW fuel cell projects.
DuPont de Nemours (DD) advanced 8.61% after beating Q3 guidance, raising its 2026 outlook, and highlighting ongoing share repurchases.
Sysco (SYY) fell 9.33% after quarterly revenue missed expectations despite an earnings beat and reaffirmed guidance related to Restaurant Depot.
Shopify (SHOP) declined 8.74% after Q3 revenue and GMV came in below forecasts, which contributed to a post-earnings selloff.
Archer-Daniels-Midland (ADM) slipped 6.82% despite Q3 earnings beating estimates and management communicating a higher 2026 adjusted EPS outlook.
US trading over the next few sessions revolves around a dense run of jobs data and inflation prints that feed directly into rate expectations and sector moves.
ADP Employment Change Wed 4 Nov. Economists look for 69K private payroll gains versus 90K previously. A figure well above that range would support the resilient demand narrative and can keep pressure on borrowing costs and rate sensitive stocks.
ISM Services PMI Wed 4 Nov. The services gauge carries a 54.8 consensus after a 54.9 prior reading. A clear break higher would be consistent with the strong Logistics Managers Index and would support cyclicals tied to US consumer and business spending.
Non Farm Payrolls and US Unemployment Rate Fri 6 Nov. Wall Street is watching a 65K payroll forecast with joblessness at 4.2%. A softer hiring print with unemployment stable would ease pressure on expectations for future rate hikes for US equities.
US Average Hourly Earnings Fri 6 Nov. Pay is expected to rise 0.3% month on month and 2.9% year on year after 0.1% and 3% previously. A cooler wage outcome would help the inflation picture and could support growth orientated stocks.
US Inflation and Core CPI Tue 10 Nov. Headline CPI is projected at 3.7% year on year with core at 2.5% after 2.6%. A print materially above those marks would reinforce a higher for longer rates view that often weighs on tech and long duration assets.
Tech has retreated over the past week, with a roughly 6.2% 7 day drop driven by selling in AI heavy names after the Democratic sweep and Texas data center concerns. Headlines around Oracle, CoreWeave and other AI infrastructure stocks show how quickly sentiment can shift when talk turns to moratoriums, tighter rules and higher borrowing costs for big builds.
If a chunk of your portfolio leans on cloud, software or AI platforms, today's ISM Services PMI is important because a firm read supports the strong demand story that has underpinned IT earnings. That can matter for whether investors stay patient with large AI capex plans.
Semiconductors : Chips under pressure despite strong backlog
Semiconductors have slipped harder than the broader Tech sector, with a roughly 7.3% 7 day decline as investors reassess how much AI server and PC demand can absorb higher memory and component costs. Stories around AMD and Intel flag PC market challenges, while SK hynix export license delays and Nvidia's tighter rules on China remind readers that policy and supply constraints sit alongside AI enthusiasm.
If you own chip ETFs or GPU exposed stocks, Friday's US Non Farm Payrolls is the one macro event to watch because a stronger hiring print can keep yields firm. That often weighs most on sectors where valuations lean heavily on future cash flows tied to big capex cycles.
Energy & Oil and Gas : Strong year now hinges on crude stocks
Energy and Oil and Gas show very strong 12 month gains of about 47% and 49%, even though 7 day returns have eased slightly and API data now point to a 5.267m barrel crude draw. Deals around refineries and midstream assets and commentary from majors like ExxonMobil and Phillips 66 keep attention on how producers and pipeline groups balance shareholder returns with new projects as diesel and supply stories move around.
If you hold US producers, refiners or LNG plays, today's EIA crude inventory report is the key sector catalyst. A clear draw can affect pump prices, inflation expectations and, through that, rate thinking that often feeds directly back into Energy positioning.
Healthcare & Pharmaceuticals & Biotech : Drug headlines support defensive role
Healthcare and the Pharmaceuticals & Biotech group are ahead of the US Market over 7 days and the past year, helped by company updates from CVS Health, Amgen, Eli Lilly and others on trial progress and guidance. The sector's earnings story is tied more to treatment need, clinical data and reimbursement than to weekly swings in consumer confidence, which is why it often holds up when rate or AI trades wobble.
If you use Healthcare as ballast alongside more cyclical holdings, Thursday's US Initial Jobless Claims and productivity data matter because they feed into how steady employer benefits budgets and public healthcare funding are likely to be as the Fed weighs how restrictive policy should stay.
Real Estate : Rates and data center debate drive splits
Real Estate is positive over the past week and up about 5.5% over 12 months, with specialty areas like data center and storage seeing very different narratives. Omega Healthcare Investors, Vornado and others are still working through funding costs, while new AI powered data center plans from utilities and landlords now have to factor in state level resistance and possible moratoriums in places like Texas.
If you own REITs that touch offices, industrial parks or data centers, the US 30 year mortgage rate update and Friday's jobs and wage figures are especially important. Stickier borrowing costs can influence both property values and refinancing terms, which flow straight through to dividends and debt service capacity.

items.summary: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt  Space<a href="https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMigwFBVV95cUxPUUxvNmNJYkR6V1Na
items.content:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory orbits above Earth in this artist's concept.
(Image credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab)
NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road.
Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit.
The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.
Swift — officially known as the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer — launched to Earth orbit in November 2004 on a two-year mission to study gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most powerful explosions in the universe . "Swift" was not an acronym but rather referred to the spacecraft's observational agility.
"Swift needed to detect and locate gamma-ray bursts, communicate their position to other observatories, and then swing its telescopes around to image the burst locations before their afterglows faded out," S. Bradley Cenko, Swift's principal investigator (PI) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, said in an Oct. 23 statement . "This typically took Swift about a minute to do."
Swift didn't just observe GRBs. It also studied a variety of other cosmic bodies and phenomena, from faraway supernova explosions and feeding black holes to asteroids and comets in our own solar system.
And it kept doing this long after its warranty expired — for about 20 years after, in fact. The space telescope didn't conduct its final science observation until this past Oct. 20 . (Swift underwent a name change during this stretch: In 2018, it was rechristened the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory after its first PI, who died the previous year.)
"Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long," Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA's Astrophysics Division, said in the same Oct. 23 statement.
"In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community," he added.
Katalyst Space's LINK robotic servicing spacecraft captured this view of one of its solar panels in Earth orbit in August 2026. (Image credit: Katalyst Space)) Swift was incredibly productive, observing more than 2,000 GRBs and 1,400 supernovas over the course of its long scientific life. But it could have gathered even more data, had a dramatic rescue mission worked out.
In September 2025, NASA awarded the Arizona company Katalyst Space a $30 million contract to design, launch and operate a robotic spacecraft that would meet up with Swift and boost it to a higher orbit, thus extending its operational life.
Swift was falling back to Earth: It had no onboard thrusters to counteract the effect of atmospheric drag, which had been pulling the observatory down ever since it launched. The process was accelerating as Swift got lower, so Katalyst had to work fast. And the company did: It launched its refrigerator-sized, three-armed LINK servicing spacecraft on July 3 , targeting an August capture of Swift.
That didn't happen, however. LINK suffered problems with its propulsion system and orientation-maintaining reaction wheels, which nixed the planned meetup. Still, it was a worthwhile effort, according to NASA.
"From the beginning, this was a high-risk, high-reward mission," Domagal-Goldman said in a statement on Sept. 25 , the day that LINK itself crashed back to Earth.
"And while we'll be sad to see Swift's mission come to a close, we knew this boost effort would be worthwhile either way — advancing U.S. spacecraft servicing technology, challenging us to meet unprecedented mission timelines, and testing how we operate satellites to extend their time in low Earth orbit ," he added.
Swift's crash today wasn't exactly unusual, by the way. At least three large objects — dead satellites or spent rocket bodies — fall back to Earth every day on average, a 2025 report found . And that number is bound to rise in the coming years, as humanity builds out more and more megaconstellations in Earth orbit.

items.content:
Americans have said 'NO TO WAR,' Iran speaker says of U.S. midterms
Ghalibaf said that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message."
The Iran war has been a central issue for voters in the midterms, after U.S. President Donald Trump launched joint strikes with Israel against the Islamic Republic in February.
Should Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, they could push through a binding War Powers Resolution, which will then direct Trump to end the conflict with Iran should Congress not authorise it.
In this handout image provided by ICANA, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf meets with Pakistan's Army Chief Syed Asim Munir (not in frame) on May 23, 2026 in Tehran, Iran.
Iran's speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Americans have said "NO TO WAR," as projections from U.S. midterm elections showed that Democrats have flipped both houses of Congress.
Posting on X after projections showed that Democrats will have a majority in the House and Senate over the coming two years, Ghalibaf said that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message."
"If the [U.S. government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
The X account of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei posted: "The process of the US's collapse has accelerated."
"If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they're gravely mistaken," the account added.
Last Saturday, Khamenei had called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
The Iran war has been a central issue for voters in the midterms, after U.S. President Donald Trump launched joint strikes with Israel against the Islamic Republic in February. The conflict has pushed up energy prices across the U.S., which has led to cost of living concerns.
Trump is also blaming the Iran war in part for the Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress, telling the Wall Street Journal that "Iran was a piece of it" when asked if the war contributed to the Republicans losses.
However, he maintains that prosecuting the war was the right decision, saying, "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again."
Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the midterm elections.
With their new majorities, Democrats might be able to push through a War Powers Resolution, which will direct Trump to end the conflict with Iran should Congress not authorize it.
In June, both chambers — which were then Republican controlled — passed a concurrent resolution to end the conflict, although a concurrent resolution is not binding and does not have the force of law. Previous attempts to impose a binding War Powers Resolution had been defeated.
